records.text: e indicator captures the totality of labour market matching – a good proxy of slack and wage bargaining power. As such, we look at five measures – each with its own pros and cons. The vacancy/unemployment ratio. This is the Beveridge Curve in ratio form. A high V/U ratio means jobs are plentiful relative to job-seekers — tight matching. A falling V/U signals either slack or better matching efficiency (more unemployed chasing fewer vacancies). It's the closest thing we may have to a matching "thermometer." The V/U ratio is more widely used as a measure of broad labour market matching as it directly maps to search-and-matching theory. However, the V/U ratio does not tell us why matching is improving/deteriorating — is it skills mismatch, geographic immobility, or just cyclical demand weakness? Moreover, changes in the V/U ratio could also be a reflection of structural changes in the economy and labour market. Where is the V/U ratio now? As of March 2026, we estimate the V/U ratio to have dropped to 0.394 — well below its peak of 1.02 in the summer of 2022. Indeed, for the given unemployed population there are far fewer vacancies – and/or matching opportunities. records.text: 1 June 2026 World Outlook Deutsche Bank AG Page 25 Japan Summary The outlook for the Japanese economy has shifted significantly since our November World Outlook, primarily due to a massive upward revision in our oil price forecast. This significant cost-push shock is expected to drive inflation higher and weigh on growth. Consequently, we have substantially raised our inflation forecast and now expect the Bank of Japan (BoJ) to pursue a more aggressive tightening cycle, with the policy rate reaching 1.75% by April 2027 through quarterly hikes starting in July 2026. While government subsidies may temporarily soften the blow, the risk of nonlinear price-setting behavior means inflation could overshoot model- based estimates. We have revised down our real GDP growth forecast for 2026 while significantly revising up our CPI inflation forecast, placing our inflation view notably above the consensus. Growth: Consumption headwinds and supply buffers The sharp rise in oil prices, stemming from heightened tensions in the Middle East since March, has already caused a significant deterioration in consumer sentiment, signaling a likely downturn in household consumption. We expect real employee compensation to decline for the remainder of the year as inflation accelerates. While a potential catch-up in next year's Shunto wage negotiations could lead to a rebound in real compensation, near-term prospects are weak. Reflecting these pressures, we have lowered our 2026 growth forecast from 0.

We see the timing of a rate hike, whether in June or July, as still being close to a 50-50 call. If a June hike is decided despite these hurdles, it would signal that the BoJ is acting out of strong concern about inflation, which we would view as a favorable sign for our medium- to long-term outlook for the BoJ. Lessons from the US and Europe's "behind-the-curve" experience Concerns are growing in financial markets that the BoJ is "behind the curve," risking a loss of control over inflation due to delayed rate hikes. We believe the BoJ has, until now, been pursuing an intentional behind-the-curve strategy (prioritizing the eradication of the deflationary mindset), and thus feel that current market concerns are somewhat excessive. The experience of the US and Europe since 2022 offers valuable insights. This strength is also being supported by the government’s fis- cal measures that effectively shoulder the inflationary pres- sures emerging globally. This week, in addition to a supple- mentary budget related to energy subsidies of more than JPY3 trillion (about 0.5% of GDP)—already signaled by the gov- ernment last week—the administration indicated it will fund fiscal costs related to the growth strategy, currently being dis- cussed under the Takaichi government, through a framework managed outside the general account. While the size and details will be clarified in due course, the government appears to be considering a scheme similar to the existing Fiscal Investment and Loan Programs (FILP). If so, future invest- ment budgets executed under this framework would, statisti- cally, be classified as belonging to a public-sector entity sepa- rate from the government, and therefore would not affect the general government’s primary balance or the outstanding government debt. Politically, this would likely be used to argue that the government is “responsibly” mindful of fiscal discipline even while pursuing an expansionary fiscal stance. Purchasing power strains show through to saving rate April’s income and spending estimates showed inflation-adjusted consumer spending rising just 0.1% m/m, with price increases accounting for nearly all of the 0.5% nominal gain. That places spending on a soft growth trajectory as we stepped into the second quarter, consistent with the downshift we have been anticipating as consumers grapple with purchasing power pressures from elevated headline inflation and the gradually slowing trajectory of aggregate labor income. That said, we think it will take some time for this to be reflected in the quarterly estimates, with revised monthly data for February and March now implying a 1.2pp carryover effect for Q2 consumer spending growth. Strains on household purchasing power are plainly evident in the saving rate. We have entered a long 2035 Coltes position as first round results shows that a market friendly outcome in the presidential race is likely . Different reasonable assumptions on vote transfer from first round candidates into runoff candidates suggests that risks are skewed for right wing candidate Abelardo de la Espriella to win . records.text: ed as an acute macroeconomic crisis, this oil shock has, so far, felt oddly more manageable, even as it marks the largest disruption to oil markets on record. Even with oil prices nearing $120 a barrel in April and May, electricity prices across most European countries continued to slip into negative territory, pushed down by massive surges in solar and wind generation. This is not to suggest that the adjustment has been painless everywhere. Globally, we track demand losses of 2.8 mbd in March, 4.3 mbd in April, and 5.6 mbd in May, while acknowledging extremely limited visibility in parts of Africa and Southeast Asia. Roughly 40-60% of the decline reflects weaker petrochemical feedstock demand, with the remainder coming from transport fuels. Even so, the broader impact on global economic activity has been relatively contained: our economists have trimmed global growth by only about 24 basis points in 2026, while raising inflation by around 100 basis points. Nor has China been immune, despite the presumed availability of large stocks of petrochemicals. China’s economic growth weakened sharply in April, and high-frequency data suggest that softness carried into May. Industrial activity slowed, while nearly every segment tied to domestic demand weakened materially. For the purposes of this analysis, we exclude the vacancy yield – given its shorter time series (2017-2026). In running our augmented Phillips curve models, we look at how each variable has contributed to wage growth. We estimate that slack alongside labour market mismatches are likely dragging on wage momentum (AWE Regular Pay) by a magnitude of -20bps to -80bps, relative to its peak (in the aftermath of the pandemic). The rest of the drop-off in pay growth can be attributed to both pay normalisation and falling household inflation expectations. The latter, we think, will be important in shaping wage growth expectations in the coming quarters – given the expected inflation wave. This is something we will be watching closely, including how matching efficiency evolves in the midst of a weakening labour market. records.text: 1 June 2026 World Outlook Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Overview 2026 continues to deliver on our promise from the last World Outlook (WO) back in November of being “anything but dull.” The world economy grapples with a complex interplay of persistent AI-driven optimism and the disruptive force of the Middle East conflict, making it feel like 1999 meets 1990, but hopefully not 1973. In our last WO, we discussed how the current technological revolution would be transformative for the globe, with an extreme differential between winners and losers. DB’s S&P 500 target of 8,000, set back in our November edition, now appears much more realistic than many expected at the time. Even so, markets, companies and countries are likely to remain highly sensitive to shifts in sentiment around AI’s impact, with large swings likely in both directions. It is worth remembering that, before the Iran war, the 2026 narrative had already swung sharply towards concerns over imminent AI driven disruption, job losses and disinflation. Only a few months on and the focus has shifted to the inflationary effects of the AI investment boom. For its beneficiaries (US, North Asia) this investment boom has helped buffer the impact of the energy shock. records.text: China Outlook Green shoots in the rear-view mirror Stabilization in the property market was short-lived with property sales weakening into May. The de-stocking cycle still faces mounting challenges amid slowing property sales. Consumption showed more signs of weakness in May with steep auto sales contraction, while exports remain a bright spot. Property market weakened into May Post the green shoots that emerged in March and early April, the high frequency data showed the property market began to weaken from late April. Growth in new property sales in 30 major cities almost stalled, posting 0.1% y/y in May versus 3% in April. The slowdown is led by lower tier cities, which reversed course, slumping 18% in tier-3 cities in May after increasing 5% in April, while the expansion in tier-1 cities narrowed significantly to 8% in May from 19% in April. We think the national property sales data could be worse than 30 major cities' data given the former covered more lower tier cities (tier 3-4 cities account for ~80% of national sales). For context, new national property sales declined 9.5% y/y in April from -7.4% in March. With weakening property sales, the de-stocking cycle still faces mounting challenges. According to CIRC data, the unsold property inventory digestion period in 80 cities has risen to 34.5 months as of end-April, up 1.8 months from end-2025, due to weaker sales. records.text: M Global Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 How Fast Can Middle East Production Recover? The puzzle, again In recent days, the front-month Brent future has fallen to about $92 a barrel. The most intriguing feature of that number is how unremarkable it is. Adjust the past twenty years of Brent prices for inflation, and today's level sits exactly at the 50th percentile of the distribution — i.e. today's price is the historic median. It is neither an exaggeration nor hyperbole that the current supply shock is the largest in history, and yet, it has produced a price that is, statistically, the most ordinary of the last two decades. It is barely above the ~$80 'mode' of this historical distribution (i.e. the price that, in real terms, has occurred most frequently) toward which we eventually expect prices to converge once the disruption has cleared. When we last wrote, in Why is the Price of Oil Not Higher? (11 May), we set out why prices had risen far less than the scale of the shock implied: the market entered the conflict with substantial buffers, it has persistently expected an imminent reopening of the Strait, and the US's high exports and China's low imports have shielded the rest of the oil market. Three weeks on, the question has, if anything, sharpened — because the price has not risen. It has fallen, from ~$104 at the time of our last note to ~$92 today. More telling than the level is the shape of the curve, and how much further it has flattened since we published on 11 May.

Not necessarily There is some evidence that bond yields can pressure equity valuations if they rise past ~4-5%, but bond volatility has a greater impact. Historical data shows that higher UST 10Y yields are typically associated with lower P/E ratios, but the relationship between yields and multiples becomes more pronounced when looking at changes over a 12-month period. records.text: 1 June 2026 Focus Europe Page 4 Deutsche Bank AG Euro area This article is an extract of the European section published in the World Outlook dated 1 June 2026 Summary: Before the energy shock, Europe's macro outlook was a "two-economy problem": domestic cyclical resilience in 2025, boosted by German fiscal spending in 2026, contrasted with a medium-term outlook clouded by weak competitiveness and lack of strategic autonomy. The stagflationary energy shock, anticipated monetary tightening, and a weaker-than-expected German fiscal multiplier have worsened the near-term outlook. Growth. Since December, we've lowered the euro area GDP forecast for 2026 to 0.5% (from 1.1%), largely due to the Middle East crisis and energy shock, alongside a weaker German fiscal multiplier. The energy shock impacts through several channels: a real income shock to consumption from higher inflation, increased uncertainty leading to lower investment and higher savings, tighter monetary policy, and reduced exports from lower global growth. This forecast assumes the Strait of Hormuz opens by mid-year, with Brent crude averaging USD93/bbl in 2026 and USD80/bbl in 2027. A more immediate reopening of the Strait would leave the 2026 GDP growth forecast at 0.5%. Either way, we would forecast a -0.1% qoq contraction in Q2 GDP, consistent with current trackers. Morgan Barrels consumed / real GDP Expenditure / nominal GDP In this note we conduct two investigations into the pass- through from energy prices into core inflation. First, we look at how overall core inflation has responded over time to ener- gy prices, controlling for the state of the business cycle. Next, we look at the energy intensiveness of individual core goods and services and see how they responded to the most recent energy shock of 2022, as an imperfect guide to what may be coming down the pike. We find that the pass-through into core PCE inflation from energy prices is small, as expected. Time series regressions imply that a 50% increase in oil prices would raise core PCE prices about 0.3-0.4%, and under a couple plausible scenarios for the future path of oil prices, core PCE is 10-15bp higher on average over 2026-27. We separately estimate that petro- leum inputs make up about 1.0% of the cost of core personal consumption, so full pass-through would imply a 50% rise in oil prices yields a 0.5% increase in core PCE prices. The administration frames the 1Q26 IFP as ‘a punto de partida’—a baseline rath- er than a policy blueprint. Formal structural balance targets will be set in a forthcoming Fiscal Policy Decree due in June 2026. The current trajectory reflects inherited obligations under current law, alongside initial corrective measures, and does not constitute the administration’s official fiscal anchors. The definitive close for 2025 confirms a sharp deterioration relative to the IFP 3Q24 baseline (which underpinned the 2025 Budget Law). The effective deficit widened by 1.8%-pt of GDP, largely due to a deeper and more persistent revenue shortfall than previously acknowledged. The structural deficit reached 3.7% of GDP, overshooting the 1.6% target by 2.1%-pt and formally triggering the corrective mechanism under the fiscal rule. The primary structural deficit stood at 2.6% of GDP, with the primary effective deficit at 1.7%. Under the Fiscal Responsibility Law, missing the structural balance target mandates immediate corrective action. records.text: US Economics 01 June 2026 Citi Research 2 Very low initial and continuing jobless claims through the mid-April to mid-May reference period suggest another month of stable labor market data in the May employment report. We expect nonfarm payroll employment to rise by 60k jobs and for the unemployment rate to remain at 4.3% (albeit alongside another decline in the labor force participation rate). This would be the third consecutive month of positive job growth but likely unsurprising to markets and Fed officials that have come to expect stability in jobs data. But we would continue to caution that monthly payroll employment changes have likely become more volatile over the last year (meaning downside surprises are not unlikely) and substantial uncertainty around labor force participation creates two-sided risks to the unemployment rate. Markets would likely be more reactive (pricing out rate hikes) to any signs of a weakening labor market (softer payrolls, higher unemployment) in May data. It remains our base case that the labor market is continuing to very gradually loosen (primarily through still-low hiring). As in previous years, we expect this to become more apparent in data through the summer, with the unemployment rate rising to 4.6-4.7% later in the year and Fed officials lowering rates in response. AI infrastructure spending is on track to reach $830 billion by year-end 2026, with hyperscalers driving nearly 90% of this growth and reshaping global capital flows. As the buildout accelerates, investor focus is moving upstream. The most important theme emerging is the AI bottleneck . This captures the handful of companies with the scale, expertise, and access to supply the critical components that keep the AI economy running. Unlike the broad software and cloud trade, this theme is defined by acute supply constraints, where only one or a few companies can deliver what is needed. Bottlenecks are most visible in high-bandwidth memory (SK Hynix, Micron, Samsung), photonics (Broadcom, Coherent), cooling management (Vertiv, Modine), energy generation, and grid infrastructure. These companies are not just suppliers, they are critical to the next phase of AI growth, with market power and technical barriers that are not easily overcome. Investors are shifting focus from capex spenders to firms that control these bottlenecks. In this cycle, the real winners will be those who own the bottleneck, as relentless demand turns scarcity into outsized returns. records.text: Box 2: Comparing Our Results Across Different Growth Databases Growth and convergence studies typically use one of four different databases when analyzing long-term economic performance: World Development Indicators (WDI) by the World Bank, the Penn World Tables (PWT), the Maddisson Project Database (MPD), and the Total Economy Database (TED) developed by the Conference Board. We generally use the Total Economy Database, partly because it provides the most up-to-date GDP figures. However, to cross-check our findings, we have replicated our analysis using each of these databases to ensure the robustness of our results. Each of these databases possesses distinct advantages and limitations, making some more suitable than others depending on the research objectives. Among them, the Maddisson database offers the most extensive historical coverage, in some cases reaching back centuries, making it ideal for studies in economic history. The World Bank’s database has the shortest historical span, beginning only in 1990. Another key distinction is how they adjust GDP figures for differences in Purchasing Power Parity (PPP), which in turn impacts growth indicators. The results of replicating our convergence analysis across each of the databases are presented in Exhibit 8. Although there are minor variations in the slopes of the fitted lines, the principal result— that weighted convergence persists—remains broadly consistent across all datasets. Excluding 597 Fifth Avenue, advances are meaningful but not dominant at 41% of liquidation expenses, and traditional workout costs (liquidation fees, special servicing fees, legal/receiver expenses, and property protection) make up the bulk of expenses. This subset is likely more representative of a typical CMBS liquidation, where advances exist but are not the dominant expense driver. Given the small sample size and the concentration effect of 597 Fifth Avenue, these decomposition results should be read as directional rather than definitive. In funding markets, repo conditions firmed modestly and moved higher after last week’s exceptionally soft levels, when both SOFR and TGCR fell to YTD lows of 3.50%—flat to the lower bound of the Fed’s target range. That softness likely reflected a buildup of RMPs over recent months, continued T-bill paydowns, strong dealer intermediation capacity, and additional cash entering the front end from the GSEs (typical seasonal flows) and growth in MMFs. It is a hybrid system where one-third of members of parliament are elected by a first-past-the-post rule and the other two-thirds are elected by party-list proportional representation. The share of proportional representation is then adjusted with a majoritarian correction that allows only coalitions/a single party with more than 10%/3% of the votes to elect their candidates. The government is considering amending the current system by dropping the first-past-the-post component and introducing a majority premium for the coalition gaining most votes and achieving at least 42% support overall. The discussion on the new system will start in Parliament on 26 June but, irrespective of the outcome, the incentive to form large coalitions is likely to remain. We think that the primary focus for investors is likely to be on the likelihood that the election delivers a clear parliamentary majority. BoE governor lays out limits of tolerance Speaking this week, Governor Bailey outlined how the current energy price shock fits into the BoE’s flexible inflation-targeting remit. He explained that the extent to which the central bank weighs depressing output and demand against inflation is not constant, but rather a function of how much of the expected inflation comes from direct, indirect and, most important, second- round effects. The higher the risk of second-round effects, the more weight should be put on inflation (the lower the infamous lambda). Linking this to the current policy debate, Bailey said that the softness of the labour market gave him confidence that he could tolerate inflation going temporarily above target. We view this as consistent with his position for the past few months: acting under uncertainty, keeping rates on hold would be the appropriate way to manage the trade-off, unless he perceives the risk of second-round effects has increased sufficiently to lower his lambda. records.text: ab 1 June 2026 Global Research US Daily Data Recap ISM manufacturing up, CPIP revised lower The ISM manufacturing index rose 1.3 points to 54.0 in May, marking a fifth straight month of expansion and the highest level in four years. Gains were broad across components. The improvement suggests solid underlying demand, though the employment index remains in contraction despite some firming. Supplier delivery times — likely boosted by supply disruptions rather than demand — are likely providing some artificial support to the headline index. The S&P Global manufacturing PMI revised down 0.2 points to 55.1 in the final May estimate. Construction spending rose 0.4% in April, slightly above expectations, though the prior two months saw notable downward revisions. Nonresidential spending was essentially flat, with data centers the only clear bright spot amid broader weakness in manufacturing plant construction and other categories. Residential construction spending rose 0.8% in April, led by single-family building, while state and local construction spending was little changed, reflecting ongoing budget constraints. The downward revisions imply softer Q1 structures investment, while April data came out in line with our expectations. records.text: 1 June 2026 World Outlook Page 30 Deutsche Bank AG India Summary: We have revised our FY27 growth forecast lower to 6.7%yoy, from 7.5%yoy before the war. If the monsoon disappoints, then real GDP growth could moderate further to 6.3%yoy. Given higher oil prices and risks of a sub-normal monsoon, we forecast CPI inflation to rise to 4.9%yoy in FY27 (from 4.3% before the war), though core CPI inflation is expected to be lower at 4.4%. Given the war, we have brought forward our rate hike call to commence from Oct-Dec’26 vs. our earlier call of the rate hike cycle starting from April 2027. At this stage, we factor in two 25bps rate hikes in Oct-Dec’26 and another 50bps cumulative rate hikes by mid-2027, taking the terminal repo rate to 6.25%. The Economic Stabilization Fund, which has a corpus of INR 1 trn (0.26% of GDP), will come in handy to deal with the fiscal slippage risks. If crude oil prices average between USD 95-100 / bbl, then the FY27 fiscal deficit target of 4.3% of GDP can still be met in our view. The rupee remains undervalued at this stage, in REER terms. In addition, fuel and retail price caps are unlikely to be main- tained indefinitely, while voluntary price freeze agreements in the services sector are also expected to unwind over time. On the fiscal side, the deficit remains wide (we forecast 6% of GDP this year), and recent statements from incoming officials suggest risks of further slippage. Moreover, while the NBH does not need to mechanically follow other central banks, external developments still act as an important constraint. We expect the ECB to continue hiking, and see risks that both the CNB and NBP may also need to tighten (not our base case, but indicative of the balance of risks). In this context, we think the NBH will proceed with the June cut—effectively delivering the second easing step it was unable to implement earlier in the year. records.text: The Turning Point for Political Risk: Factors to Watch Political stability, a key feature supporting the constructive macroeconomic landscape in Italy since 2022, is coming under closer scrutiny as the 2027 general elections loom. After the government’s constitutional reform was rejected in a referendum last March, the recent round of local elections (24 and 25 May) delivered a more balanced outcome, with centre-right candidates slightly outperforming opinion polls. However, over the last three months, opinion polls have pointed to some erosion in political support for the ruling coalition. PM Meloni’s party (Fratelli d’Italia) still polls above the share of votes it received in the 2022 election, a rare feature for a government that has been in office for almost 4 years, but support for the ruling coalition (which includes Lega and Forza Italia) has weakened since the beginning of the year. The downtrend accelerated further after the recent defection of some far-right MPs from the ruling coalition to establish a new fringe party (Futuro Nazionale). Futuro Nazionale, currently polling around 4%, seems to be attracting votes from Lega and Fratelli d’Italia in the coalition government (Exhibit 4), based on a similar 4% decline in support for the coalition. The design of the Italian electoral system incentivizes large coalition building among different parties ahead of elections. It is a hybrid system where one-third of members of parliament are elected by a first-past-the-post

records.text: 1 June 2026 World Outlook Page 16 Deutsche Bank AG inflation staying above 2% throughout 2027, indicating a persistent inflation shock. Surveys since the energy shock show a strong pass-through of rising input costs to manufacturing output prices, suggesting upside risks to core goods inflation. Services selling prices are also rising despite weakening demand, indicating pricing power. Bargaining power is ambiguous. The vacancies-to-unemployment ratio and labor shortages, while not as high as in 2022, haven't normalized. The cumulative real income shock of almost 2 percentage points over 2026-2027 suggests workers may seek to recoup losses. Our dbDIG survey shows increased household intent to ask for pay raises since the energy shock, but labor demand is cooling, and unemployment fears are rising. Conversely, weak purchasing power may cap persistent inflation. Fiscal policy offers only partial, temporary protection against the real income shock, and bank- based financial conditions are tightening, with the BLS forecasting a sharp Q2 tightening. Tracking the energy shock's inflation transmission: direct effects are normal. Like 2022, indirect effects might take six months to become clear; nothing obvious in the first two months. Wage inflation, a classic second-round effect, could take 6-12 months to assess. Household inflation expectations show some increase, another second-round effect, but whether this dissipates with falling oil prices remains to be seen. Monetary Policy.

records.text: • Last year’s debt brake reform allows for much more expansionary fiscal policy, but constraints still exist • Further reforms are being considered, which could tighten the debt brake modestly again • Reforms are for the longer-term, but a transition could begin to bite in the next 3-4 years Last year’s far-reaching reform of the German debt brake often gives the impression that fiscal constraints have been entirely lifted. That is true only up to a point and EU fiscal rules must also be adhered to. The government has pledged to “modernise” the debt brake to protect public capex once the Special Fund for Infrastructure runs out and to ensure that public debt is eventually put back on a declining path. An Expert Commission is working on proposals, but seems to be struggling to make progress. Overall, some of last year’s loos- ening of the debt brake could be reversed, although a long transition period would not affect the large 2% fiscal easing over 2026/27. Even with some “modernisation”, the govern- ment will eventually have to make large budget savings. The debt brake ain’t gone Last year, the government pushed through three key reforms of the debt brake. As is clear from the equation above, the relative magnitude of the government’s average interest rate and nominal GDP growth is key to the “r - g” effect. Exhibit 2 shows that when Japan fell into a deflationary trap in the 1990s, the average interest rate exceeded nominal GDP growth for a sustained period, but since the COVID-19 pandemic, nominal GDP growth has exceeded the average interest rate due to the significant acceleration in inflation. In other words, from the late 1990s to the mid-2010s, Japan was in a phase of “natural increase” (i.e. r > g) where the public debt-to-GDP ratio increase even without a government deficit, whereas since the COVID-19 pandemic, it has been in a phase of “natural decrease” (i.e. r < g) marked by a continuous natural decline in the ratio. As a pos- sible guide, the Bundesbank has made some proposals, which have been debated by the Expert Commission. This would let the current fiscal trajectory run until 2029 as planned, fol- lowed by a six-year transition period to a reformed debt brake from 2036 onwards. This would ensure that debt peaks at 75% in 2032-33 and then drifts down to below 70% by 2040, rather than rising linearly to 90% by then. In the Bundesbank’s proposal, the final arrangement from 2036 would allow an additional 0.8% of GDP as a deficit for government capex, effectively continuing the annual flow of capex from the Special Fund for Infrastructure. The existing 0.35% structural deficit allowance for other parts of the bud- get would be allowed in full only if government debt is below 60% of GDP. If debt is higher, the structural allowance for both the federal and state budgets would be reduced to 0.1% of GDP. Hence, the structural deficit allowance would be raised to 1% of GDP when debt is above 60% (0.8% + 0.1% + 0.1%) and to 1.5% when debt is below 60% (0.8% + 0.35% + 0.35%). Historically (based on 2021–2025 averages), MMF AUMs tend to decline by roughly $90bn around the June tax date, while reserves typically fall by about $100bn—both moves meaningfully smaller than what we usually see around April tax sea- son. Separately, SOMA Manager Robert Perli provided details on the Fed’s framework for reserve management purchases (RMPs) and the factors that guide their pace. He empha- sized that the Fed’s primary objective is to keep reserves comfortably within the ample range, and said decisions on the size of RMPs are informed by three equally important con- siderations. First, policymakers assess the expected supply of reserves. records.text: 1 June 2026 World Outlook Deutsche Bank AG Page 39 Emerging Markets We had started 2026 with a glass half full view of emerging markets as an asset class, one based on a combination of tailwinds from global fiscal policy growth beta, peak tariff noise, and domestic real rate compression; and underwritten by policy prudence and a structural bid to diversify away from dollar assets. Then came the energy price shock. Our relatively constructive bias on EM has held up thus far, though it’s been tough to beat the risk beta, with the stagflationary risks from this shock getting progressively priced into both central bank reaction functions and rates term premia. EM equities have handsomely outperformed global (with North Asia the dominant contributor); EM local (blended) yield spread to USTs is flat to versus before the Middle East conflict (though wider by 20bp ytd); EMFX spot is mostly flat to start of the year; and EMBI Global spread modestly tighter. Three aspects of the fallout from the energy price shock on EM which are worth highlighting. One, the geographical dispersion. The shock has impacted Asia a lot more severely than it has other EM geographies, given both the higher energy import intensity of the region, but also that bulk of that dependence is linked to the Middle East. With policy opting in most instances in the region to dampen the transmission of the price shock to households and industry; there has been progressively bigger burden posed on fiscal balance sheets.

This resulted in a €7.4bn cyclical deficit allowance, lower than the €18.2bn in the Budget Plan (see Table 1 and 2). The structural allowance remains the same at €15.2bn as it is still based on the prior year’s nominal GDP level times the cyclical budget elasticity of 0.203. Together with slightly lower-than-planned financial transactions, the allowed deficit declined from €49.8bn in the 2025 Budget plan to €37.9 based on actual outturns. The actual deficit, excluding defence spending above 1% of GDP, was €38.3bn, which exceeded the adjusted allowed deficit by €0.4bn. This overshoot is deducted from the control account, which remains well stocked from prior years and therefore does not have to be corrected. In other words, the core part of the debt brake remains in place and must still be adhered to. The actual federal deficit in 2025 was almost €15bn smaller than planned. Some of this reflected a €3.4bn shortfall in defence spending versus the planned amount but the main part is considered a cyclical improvement (i.e. reflecting stronger growth in nominal GDP than projected in the Budget Plan). The resulting structural deficit after all exclusions was close to the deficit allowed by the debt brake. • Last year’s debt brake reform allows for much more expansionary fiscal policy, but constraints still exist • Further reforms are being considered, which could tighten the debt brake modestly again

By now, this implies five consecutive months of low imports (i.e. Apr–Aug), and with that, likely sustained inventory draws. However, there is a meaningful probability, in our view, that Chinese crude buyers may return to market for the September-delivery cycle in order to stem inventory declines. Buying for September delivery typically starts in mid/late June. If the Strait opens soon, this can happen without tightening the market. However, if that prospect continues to slip, this too provides an upside risk. Exhibit 14: Spot crude supply deals into China have been running at unusually low levels for April and May delivery, and are also still very low for Jun-Aug. records.text: Filippo Taddei +44(20)7774-5458 | filippo.taddei@gs.com Goldman Sachs International European Daily: Italy — Political Stability Comes Under Closer Scrutiny 1 June 2026 | 4:40AM BST Italian growth momentum has tracked the Euro area. While the government has n been more proactive than others in cutting fuel excise duties and pushing for EU-level energy, overall fiscal guidance remains cautious, with deficit targets below most Euro area countries in 2026-27. Despite the ongoing energy shock, there is no sign of Italy-specific economic n stress. Growth is likely to be among the weakest in the Euro area, but contained deficits mean sovereign spreads reflect broader European weakness rather than domestic risk. Political stability, a pillar since 2022, is increasingly under scrutiny ahead of the n 2027 general election. Recent local elections and polls suggest some erosion in support for the ruling coalition. The key questions are whether the opposition can unite and whether the electoral system is reformed. Our base case remains government continuity and broadly on-track delivery of n the Recovery Fund. Although Italy is more exposed to higher energy prices, low fiscal and political risks continue to support BTPs, even as spreads have already retraced much of their post-conflict widening. And, just as in the US, the roll forward in earnings combined with small upgrades means that while equities have bounced from the lows valuation is not at peaks. First, inflation is low (0.6% in April) and well below the mid-point of the target range. Second, the weight of energy in the Swiss CPI is half of that in the Eurozone and electricity pricing is regulated, implying less upward pressure from higher energy prices. Third, the SNB faces not just an energy price shock but also disinflationary pressures from CHF strength, with labour market slack leaving the economy vulnerable to downside growth risks. The SNB, in our view, has made it clear that it is primarily concerned about disinflation due to CHF strength rather than higher inflation. We believe the weakening of the CHF since the March meeting will likely be viewed by the SNB as a successful translation of its intended policy stance and hence we do not necessarily see the outlook tilted towards rate hikes. That said, the SNB will likely take into account any ECB rate hikes (which we expect in June and September 2026). After all, the ECB-SNB rate differential would widen starting this summer, potentially weaken CHF and thereby raising Swiss inflation. This could ultimately open a window for the SNB to normalize policy somewhat and move away from its 0% policy rate. Hence we expect the SNB to raise its policy rate in June 2027. Our conclusion from last year was simple “Europe just needs to deliver”. So, 13 months later, where do we stand? To jump right to the finding: Almost all investors we met this week were still looking for reasons to add Europe, so the window of opportunity still seems open. But scepticism dominates now. Third, a 0.35% structural deficit allowance was granted to the German states, who previously had to run a balanced budget at all times in structural terms. This mirrors the leeway that already exists at the federal level. Table 1 illustrates the standard debt brake calculation. The allowed structural deficit in 2026 is the prior year’s nominal GDP level times 0.35%, which equals €15.2bn. On top of this, the government is allowed to let the automatic stabilizers work, i.e. run a cyclical deficit. This is calculated as the out- put gap, currently estimated at -1.8% of GDP, times a cyclical multiplier of 0.203, which gives a cyclical deficit allowance of €15.6bn. On top of this, the debt brake allows certain financial transactions, currently budgeted at €9.6bn for 2026. These three items equate to a total federal deficit allowance of €40.4bn for 2026. The actual budget plan sees a 2026 budget deficit of €98bn, of which €57.6bn is defence spending above the 1% of GDP that still counts towards the debt brake. The planned deficit relevant for the debt brake is €40.4bn, i.e. €98bn minus €57.6bn, matching the allowed deficit. While USMCA would remain in effect if negotiations extend past the deadline, we n think markets will continue to grapple with a USMCA exit as a credible risk given the process the last time around. We expect ongoing talks will likely proceed bilaterally with US-Canada talks proving more difficult, mirroring the original USMCA process and the 2025 fentanyl-related tariffs. We construct an index of “trade conflict” headlines, measured as a share of total n trade-related news articles, which suggests that negotiations with Canada were more contentious than those with Mexico. We find that increasing trade tensions affect CAD in both spot markets—via US-Canada rate differentials—and in low-delta options, with less impact on realized or implied ATM volatility. We see three key market implications. First, USMCA negotiations are likely to be n more strained with Canada and therefore a more important driver for CAD than MXN. The agricultural output prices series is outrightly weak, at -5.4% y/y in March. This highlights a key difference to the shock in 2022, when Ukraine was a major food producer. In the latest shock, the transmission to food prices occurs through fertilizer and transport costs, so we expect it to take longer to show up. This in part is a reflection of a rising NAIRU alongside weak cyclical factors. Wage growth, we expect, will drop to 3.25% (AWE Regular Pay) by year-end. And despite a bump in CPI we anticipate weak wage bargaining power to result in a plateauing of wage settlements nearer 3.25-3.5%. Inflation: An inflation wave is all but inevitable later this year. Higher energy prices will continue to feed through into inflation over summer, as the Ofgem Price Cap raises dual fuel bills by 13% through summer. Forward curves for oil remain higher for longer too – adding to some inflation persistence. The bad news? We are seeing a broadening out of price pressures, with food prices likely to step up later this year, and some core goods inflation likely to lift in the coming months. What's the good news? Despite the coming inflation wave, domestic price pressures remain well behaved. The all-important April services print - which will set the tone for core services prices for the next 12 months undershot Bank expectations. And with wage momentum still under check, we expect to see a bifurcation in the price data – with plateauing services CPI coinciding with rising non-core CPI. During the 2022 general election, the opposition ran with three separate coalitions, which meant that its candidates had little chance of winning in the race for first-past-the-post. If the opposition had run as a united coalition, its share of votes could have been higher than the centre-right coalition currently in government. The latest opinion polls point to a similar distribution of votes across the opposition parties and suggest that a united opposition would have a much greater chance of success in the election. In particular, a ‘Broad’ coalition of the centre-left parties, 5Star and Italia Viva, the centrist party led by former PM Matteo Renzi, has almost a 5% lead over the ruling coalition, according to the latest opinion polls. If the other centrist party Azione were to join the opposition coalition (‘Largest’), the lead could approach double digits (Exhibit 5). The ‘Largest’ opposition option remains unlikely at present given the recent statement by the Azione leader, former Minister of Economic Development Carlo Calenda. That said, the outcome of general elections is clearly not just a question of simple electoral algebra. We should be wary of taking current opinion polls at face value while coalition building is still work in progress. Right after Colombia, the focus is likely to shift towards Peru, which will also hold a highly polarized run-off between the right-wing candidate Keiko Fujimori and the leftist Roberto Sanchez on June 7. An Ipsos poll shows a small edge for Fujimori (Figure 2); however, it still seems too close to call, as her lead has been mainly because of an increase in proportion of undecideds, which currently stands around 26%, rather than her gaining momentum. With this back drop, the Presidential debate that will take place this Sunday could be a catalyst for undecideds to take a position and start to provide more clarity about the path ahead. This is the strongest starting position that Fujimori has had in any of her four runoff bids, and demographics might play in her favor which has been generating hopes that she might make it this time (see Peru: Could this time be different?). However, given that her rejection levels still remain elevated and there is a strong anti-stablishment sentiment, it is still unclear if this would be her luck fourth. Global Markets Strategy Global Fixed Income Markets Weekly 29 May 2026 J P M O R G A N Potential Revisions to the JGB Issuance Plan Also in Focus According to materials for the FY2026 JGB issuance plan released last December (Link), the MoF indicated that a mid-year hearing would be conducted as part of efforts to strength- en communication with market participants. Market attention will be on whether this is dis- cussed at forums such as the June Primary Dealer (PD) meeting. Separately, at the government debt management study group held in May, the MoF dis- cussed term premia in addition to the expansion of retail JGB issuance ( Link, Japanese only). While it is important to avoid excessive shortening of issuance, there is also an increasing need to restrain duration supply. From the MoF’s perspective, efforts are likely to focus on mitigating the impact of Prime Minister Takaichi’s expansionary fiscal stance on the JGB market. However, if total issuance continues to increase, there is a risk that such measures could reach their practical limits. Against this backdrop, market attention will likely focus on whether any changes to the JGB issuance plan are announced from July onward. Consumers drive improved sentiment The European Commission’s Economic Sentiment Indicator (ESI) increased by 0.3pts in May, reaching 93.5, surpassing consensus expectations for an unchanged reading. This improvement stands in contrast to last week’s Flash PMI, which showed a further significant decline and signaled eco- nomic stagnation. The EC survey is currently providing a somewhat more optimistic view of economic momentum than the PMI; however, this divergence is typical during periods of slowdown. Overall, we place greater emphasis on the PMI, as it tends to better track activity. Among the largest economies, sentiment improved in Germany (+1pt), France (+0.9pt), and Italy (+0.1pt), but edged lower in Spain (-0.1pt). Confidence declined in manufacturing (-0.3pts), construction (-0.8pts), and retail (-0.9pts), while it strengthened in services (+0.8pts) and among consumers (+1.6pts). Labor market – A jobless outlook, even without activity slowing. The French labor market is set to weaken. We forecast the unemployment rate will rise from 7.7% in 2025 to 8.1% in 2026, before stabilizing at 8.2% in 2027. This deterioration is driven by more than just a cyclical slowdown; it reflects the unwinding of a major post- pandemic productivity gap. French employment has been running significantly above its pre-COVID trend relative to output. We estimate that had the prior productivity trend continued, employment today would be approximately 840,000 jobs lower. As this gap narrows, it will put downward pressure on job creation, a structural headwind now compounded by slowing economic activity, policy uncertainty, the dampening effect of AI, and a technical increase in jobless claims from the 2023 labor reform. Looking beyond the forecast horizon, this dynamic will eventually collide with unfavorable demographics, suggesting the historical relationship between GDP and employment is likely to evolve significantly. Inflation – An energy shock without the same underlying fire. We expect the Gulf war-induced surge in energy prices will lift French headline inflation to 2.4% on average in 2026, before it moderates to 1.9% in 2027. The weakness in government investment largely reflected a slowdown in weapons systems spending after a surge through late 2025. Over the past two quarters, real GDP fell by 0.6% on a two-quarter annualised basis, but final domestic demand still grew by 1.1%, with almost all of that growth driven by the consumer. The question now is whether consumption can hold up and whether other components can improve enough to support growth in coming quarters. records.text: at without the inflation risks stemming from the Middle East conflict, the Riksbank would likely be cutting interest rates. After all, inflation will likely continue to undershoot for the remainder of the year, partly due to tax cuts (food and energy) but also because of last year's SEK appreciation and subdued underlying price pressures. However, amid the direct and indirect inflationary effects of the energy shock we see the Riksbank on hold throughout this year. If anything, the May meeting minutes underline that the Riksbank sees the risks to the rate outlook skewed to the upside, with all board members emphasizing their readiness to raise rates if the inflation outlook warranted it. We believe for Riksbank rate hikes this year, either an unexpected broadening of price pressures beyond energy or sharp SEK depreciation would be necessary. Neither is unlikely to materialize by the time of the June meeting but are more risk factors for later in the year. In the absence of these, we do think the next rate move will be a rate hike, yet not in 2026 as indicated by market pricing but only in June 2027. To assess whether we need to bring this hike forward, we will closely watch (i) energy and producer prices, (ii) inflation expectations, (iii) the breadth of inflation pressures, (iv) hard and soft growth data with a particular focus on consumption-related indicators, and (v) SEK developments. records.text: Canada Economic Perspectives1 June 2026 ab 4 Despite energy boost, core inflation has been weaker than expected Headline inflation rose to 2.8% year on year in April, up 0.4pp from 2.4% in March, and we expect it to edge up again to 2.9% in May. Almost all of the increase has come from components directly affected by the recent rise in energy prices. Petrol prices rose 9.0% on the month in April after increasing by 21.2% in March. Prices for water, fuel and electricity rose 5.5% on the month, driven by a 41.3% increase in fuel oil and other fuels after a 21.5% rise in March. There was also a 24.6% increase in fuel, parts and accessories for recreational vehicles in April. The Bank of Canada has highlighted the risk that higher energy prices could feed into food prices through transport costs and potential disruption to fertiliser supplies, but there is little sign of that so far. Food prices fell by 0.1% on the month in April, following a 0.4% rise in March. On a year-on-year basis, food prices were up 3.5% in April, down from 4.0% in March. Another possible channel for spillover would be transport services such as air fares. However, air transport prices fell by 3.6% on the month in April on a non-seasonally adjusted basis and were down 1.7% on the year. Alongside the lack of clear spillover from the energy shock, core inflation has also been weaker than expected. The Q1 monetary policy report said the PBoC would “steer the overnight rate to operate near the policy-rate level“, suggesting a gradual upward pull of DR001 (currently 1.36%) toward the policy rate (1.40%). The PBoC has been slowly draining liquidity from March. We view the PBoC's recent actions on the medium-term lending facility (MLF) and outright reverse-repo facilities as fine-tuning the liquidity structure and normalising excessive liquidity, without changing its accommodative stance. The PBoC is less likely to cut rates this year but there is room for more fiscal policy: The Q1 2026 monetary-policy report removed the statements about RRR and policy-rate reductions. In addition, banks' net-interest margins dropped to a record low of 1.4% in Q1, which will continue to constrain the PBoC from cutting interest rates (see China: Politburo offers no hint of additional easing, dated 29 April 2026). Consequently, if growth in May remains below 4.5%, we expect policymakers to react by speeding up fiscal policy rather than lowering policy rates via monetary easing. Moreover, the July Politburo meeting could be a window for the government to announce additional fiscal stimulus if economic growth disappoints expectations. PPI reflation is not transitory: China‘s PPI inflation is more sensitive to supply than demand, and supply has tightened in many ways. records.text: 1 June 2026 Focus Europe Page 18 Deutsche Bank AG United Kingdom This article is an extract of the UK section published in the World Outlook dated 1 June 2026 Summary: We have upgraded our 2026 GDP outlook on the back of a slightly stronger Q1-26. Indeed, we think the UK economy entered the Iran energy shock on a stronger footing. Stockpiling will also support activity as the lagged energy effects feed into inflation (and thus real disposable incomes). We remain cautious on the outlook from summer, as inflation bites into spending. Political uncertainty will also rear its head again, dampening investment and housing activity. Overall, we see GDP growth this year of 1% with activity rising to 1.2% next year and 1.6% in 2028. GDP: We expect GDP growth this year to just about hit 1% - a 0.1pp upgrade from our previous forecast update. Despite higher for longer energy prices, base effects and a strong Q1-26 will leave activity running a little stronger than we previously expected. What's driving the change in growth? A stronger Q1-26, with the UK topping the G7 league table on GDP growth (0.6% q-o-q). Some catchup post Budget uncertainty plus stockpiling in the manufacturing sector as the Iran energy shock unfolded helped push GDP higher than expectations. And we expect some marginal uplift in cyclical borrowing, on the back of a weaker economy (including some targeted modest fiscal support). records.text: expected at least one dissenting vote for a hike from Mr Ryoo Sangdai and potentially another from Dr Chang Yongsung, we believe the meeting outcome was still more hawkish than our expectation. The BoK's growth and inflation forecasts were revised notably higher and the financial stability problems were also highlighted. Our baseline view remains that the first hike will be in August, though we note the July meeting as a close call. April IP data was softer than expected with broad-based slowdown across production, retail sales, services, construction, and facilities investments. If the May data is also flattish as we expect, we believe this will strengthen the case for an August hike (April activity: Slower than expected, 29 May 2026). We also think the pace will be a hike every other meeting (i.e., quarterly). The median point in the six-month dot plots suggests a rate hike every other meeting into end-2026. While the two most hawkish dots imply at least one set of back-to-back hikes, we think this outcome is unlikely, especially considering that there are also two dots for a 2.5% policy rate six months out. We also do not see any strong push for a steep hiking cycle, given that the move up in rates would start from a relatively neutral policy rate. Unless inflation trends much above 3.5% and inflation expectations start to become un-anchored, we believe the hiking pace is likely to be quarterly. We also expect the BoK's preference will point towards a terminal rate of ~3%

Across Europe and Japan, governments accelerated the buildout of nuclear power, expanded public transportation systems, improved building insulation standards, and diversified away from oil in electricity generation. The crisis also reshaped industrial processes, encouraged smaller and more fuel-efficient vehicles, and ultimately reduced the share of oil in the global energy mix over the following decades (Figures 1 & 2). This raises the key question for today: should we expect structural changes of similar magnitude from the current shock? Possibly yes, but the direction of change may be different. The 1973 crisis pushed economies to use energy more efficiently. Two major wars involving large oil producers over the past five years could accelerate something broader: the steady decoupling of economic activity from oil consumption itself. • Gasoline demand may prove to be one of the clearest examples of crisis-driven behavioral adaptation. When fuel is scarce and prices surge, consumers and firms often respond by accelerating changes already underway: efficiency improvements, modal substitution, and adoption of alternative drivetrains. China sits at the center of this dynamic. More telling than the level is the shape of the curve, and how much further it has flattened since we published on 11 May. The front-week Brent CFD — the clearest read on prompt physical tightness — has more than halved over those three weeks, from $5.7/bbl to $2.6, while the M1–M2 spread has fallen from $3.8/bbl to under $1. In other words, since our last note the market has not merely remained sanguine about a resolution — it has grown more so, increasingly pricing a clean and near-term return of supply across the whole curve. From current levels, we think that is too optimistic. We previously modelled the Strait to re-open from end-May onwards, but move this assumption to late June. On top of that, we allow for another few weeks for mine clearing, confidence building and other issues, putting the moment where exports start to inflect higher only by late July. As a result, the tightness ahead is likely deeper and more drawn-out than we initially expected, and also than the curve implies. On that timeframe, the mechanisms by which the oil market has absorbed the supply shock may become challenged. On that basis we are holding our forecasts for Dated Brent at $100 in 3Q but make modest upwards revisions for 4Q (from $90 to $95) and 1Q27 (from $80 to $85), still expecting convergence to $80 thereafter. In addition, with Sato—who is seen by the market as a dovish member—set to replace Nakagawa from July, there appears to be a growing sense of urgency among the more hawkish Board members to move ahead with a rate hike. Against this backdrop, market participants are likely left to monitor (1) developments in the Middle East, (2) indications of the severity of supply constraints, (3) Governor Ueda’s speech at the Kisaragi-kai on June 3 (17:30–18:15), and (4) media signaling ahead of the June meeting. Accordingly, we acknowledge upside risk to our call for just two hikes of 25bps and will be watching carefully for any signs on 11 June that the ECB might deliver its second hike already on 23 July and not wait until 10 September as our baseline would imply. We think that the ECB will most likely refrain from sending a strong signal regarding its July rate decision. However, if it were to signal that the next hike will already come on 23 July, we would need to decide whether (a) we bring our September hike forward (while sticking to the call that the ECB will hike only twice) or (b) add a July hike as a third hike. At this stage, we have an open mind. That said, we think the outcome will be data-dependent, with a particular focus on the data that we compiled in our heatmap on page 3 (Figure 4). Amongst these, we think inflation expectations and wage indicators will be particularly important as an early gauge of potential second-round effects; we believe any indications that Eurozone growth is slowing sharply, including employment data, would also be important for the ECB. Risks to our projections are skewed to the downside. Indeed, higher oil prices and a broadening of inflationary pressures could hit sentiment and spending faster than pencilled in with real disposable incomes squeezed by more than projected. Labour Market : The UK labour market remains weak. After a very short lived rebound to start the year, hiring plans have levelled off. The jobless rate in March pushed back to 5%. The underemployment rate is higher at around 8.5%. And the share of marginally attached workers in the labour market sits at a cyclical high of 22.5%. Labour flow data underscore the weak labour market state: job churn is back to below-normal levels and the UK quits rate has receded meaningfully. Higher frequency data remain markedly weak too with job vacancies down to their lowest level in six years. Elevated domestic and geopolitical uncertainty will do very little to quench business concerns. We expect the jobless rate to peak at 5.4% in late summer. This in part is a reflection of a rising NAIRU alongside weak cyclical factors. Wage growth, we expect, will drop to 3.25% (AWE Regular Pay) by year-end. And despite a bump in CPI we anticipate weak wage bargaining power to result in a plateauing of wage settlements nearer 3.25-3.5%. Inflation: An inflation wave is all but inevitable later this year. Right shift in Election bolds well for Coltes: A swing to the right could benefit the Coltes curve, as the market may price in an improved fiscal outlook and more balanced economic growth. The current Coltes curve reflects a high premium due to past fiscal and political uncertainty (Figure 1). Foreign holdings of Coltes are likely to be a significant factor in a potential reduction in premium, as they have been gradually decreasing their exposure to the Coltes market over the past few years, largely due to concerns regarding fiscal and political uncertainty. The sharp increase in foreign holdings from August to December 2025 can be attributed to the TRS operation and a private placement. If these factors are excluded, the current foreign holdings of 22.7% as of January 2025 would be much lower than the 24% recorded in January 2022 (Figure 2). We continue to believe that the pendulum can swing back to the centre-right/right after four years of a leftist government. As in other Latam countries, a deterioration in security conditions is an important concern for voters (Figure 3). The political centre-right/right has the upper hand here given its effective track record in addressing security issues. Other key topics include corruption and the outlook for the national healthcare system, areas where the incumbent coalition is disadvantaged as the deterioration occurred on its watch (particularly in healthcare). records.text: Exhibit 2 compares the GDP per capita of the eight most populous countries. The US is fixed as the ‘frontier economy’ in the left panel, while developed economies (excluding the US) are set as the benchmark in the right panel. China has seen significant income convergence, rising from just over 2% of US levels in 1980 to around 33% today. Since the late 1990s, India, Indonesia, and Bangladesh have also shown clear progress. When compared to US GDP per capita, Brazil, Pakistan, and Nigeria have underperformed, with Brazil slipping further behind the US over time, while Pakistan and Nigeria have remained largely unchanged. However, as the US has shown particularly strong performance among developed markets, the relative picture shifts if we compare these economies to developed markets more broadly – Pakistan and Nigeria now show some convergence, whereas Brazil has remained more or less flat.3 3 The aim of this piece is to record, rather than explain, the convergence that has occurred. However, the question remains as to why the GDP per capita performance of Brazil, Pakistan and Nigeria has been disappointing. In Brazil’s case, macroeconomic instability, high government spending crowding out private investment, significant trade barriers and inadequate infrastructure are all cited as contributing factors. Instead, it stated that the "current level of the policy rate gives the Riksbank a good initial position to adjust monetary policy if required to safeguard the inflation target." It openly acknowledged that growth in Q1 had been weak ( with GDP contracting 0.2% q/q in Q1) and current inflation is running well below the 2% target (headline at 0.8% y/y, core at 0.0% in April) after repeated downside surprises in recent months. This gives the Riksbank "scope to wait until there is a clearer picture of the effects of the war". However, it also emphasised that "risks of higher inflation going forward have increased somewhat"; and the statement conveyed a modest tightening bias, because it only mentioned a potential increase in the policy rate, no cut. records.text: Marvin Loh29 May 2026 1 Insights Classification: Complimentary Material Developed Markets Strategy Weekly: Buying the rumour, questioning the newsKEY THEMES THIS WEEK: Excuse our scepticism. Another week, another peace deal. We are inclined to contain our enthusiasm that the world will return to more sane footing until after we hear confirmation from all three parties on deal progress. While remaining guarded, we do think that limiting additional hostilities while working on a deal is a positive outcome. Risk assets approve, as do the rates markets, although some of this initial enthusiasm faded into post-holiday trading. Our real money flows support some of this hesitancy, with the Behavioural Risk Score falling to neutral after remaining mostly risk on during the conflict. Additional cautionary signals come from BRS internals, with narrowing equity risk taking and rising cash levels. The latter has had a notable impact on funding levels, which are at their cheapest levels in years, a possible sign of liquidity hoarding in the face of uncertain market dynamics. These cross-currents frame our neutral approach to the portfolio this week, which we are leaving unchanged with a series of relative value and idiosyncratic trade ideas. Still hawkish, just a little less. Monetary Policy. Pre-energy shock, we expected the ECB to keep rates at 2% – around neutral – through 2026 before hiking gradually from mid-2027 to a modestly restrictive stance (2.75% in 2028) as inevitable fiscal spending on strategic autonomy, a tightening labour market and geopolitical frictions (including protectionism) tilt the balance of risks towards medium-term inflation. AI, the Second China Shock and euro appreciation remain counter-arguments. We now anticipate a 50bp hike to 2.50% in summer 2026, the upper end of the neutral range. This is seen as 'measured' tightening and good risk management, signaling commitment to price stability without overly burdening growth. President Lagarde has outlined the ECB reaction functions: (1) 'look through' if the inflation impact is small and temporary, (2) 'measured' tightening if the inflation shock is large but not too persistent, and (3) 'forceful or persistent' tightening if the shock is significant and sustained. Given projected headline inflation peaking at 3.7%, a cumulative inflation shock of almost 2 percentage points over 2026-2027, and persistence risks, we believe the ECB will implement 'measured' tightening, even if the Strait of Hormuz opens soon. While the Fed acknowledges that this inflation shock could be temporary, there is a risk that the persistence of positive shock could alter the perception of the zero-mean nature of the shock, putting upward pressure on inflation expectations. The Fed’s Waller described a “Bayesian” way to think about inflation shocks as the continuous updating of beliefs: even if each individual price jump is, in principle, temporary, a run of similar shocks can prompt households and businesses to increase the odds they assign to persistently higher inflation, drawing on recent experience. He argues that this kind of repeated updating can push inflation expectations upward, making it harder for policymakers to dismiss shocks as noise because once people infer a pattern and start treating higher inflation as the new baseline, bringing inflation back down becomes more difficult and the policy reaction function may need to respond more assertively. We expect central banks to continue to shift more hawkish, but also anticipate any rate hikes in response to the conflict to be modest. records.text: There is renewed interest in the sustainability of Japan’s public debt following a n sharp rise in market interest rates on Japanese government bonds (JGBs) against the backdrop of rising inflation and fiscal risk premiums. When considering the sustainability of public debt, two factors must be n examined: future trends in interest rates and nominal GDP growth (the so-called “r - g” effect), and the trend in the primary balance. The “r - g” effect refers to the phenomenon whereby the debt-to-GDP ratio n (debt/GDP ratio) naturally declines when the government’s average interest rate (aggregate interest expenses/total debt) is lower than the nominal GDP growth rate. Over the past few years, the government’s interest rate has been significantly below the nominal GDP growth rate, and as a result, the debt/GDP ratio has rapidly declined from 260% in FY2020 to 220% in FY2024, despite continued primary balance deficits. Even if market interest rates remain at their current elevated levels, the n government’s interest rate (average across all liabilities) would only rise gradually. Therefore, for the next few years, the natural decline in the debt/GDP ratio would likely continue at 2-3 pp, and the ratio would continue its downward trend. However, if market interest rates were to remain high for a prolonged period, the n government interest rate could eventually rise significantly and exceed the nominal GDP growth rate. Worsening sentiment (i.e., re-escalation) would likely trigger a bigger sell-off in the swap curve than in the bond curve, echoing March’s sharp spread compression. With spreads already near pre-conflict levels (Figure 1), we see ample room to tighten should this scenario unfold. A credible peace deal might initially push the asset swap spread wider, but any widening should be modest. The swap curve has limited downside, and a strong peso lifts bonds more than swaps, curbing the potential spread increase. With Banxico already near its terminal rate and oil price driven inflation risk, a sharp rally that drives long end swaps below pre conflict levels looks unlikely. Moreover, the MXN has outperformed its historical oil beta during the current shock—a pattern we expect to continue as the U.S. economy remains resilient. A strong peso also limits the spread’s ability to widen meaningfully in a de escalation scenario. Lastly, if the ceasefire does hold and the status quo persists, the spread still appears wide after recent local curve rallies. We expect the bond curve to gradually close the gap with the swap curve, helped by the strong peso that favors bonds and a likely consolidation of the swap curve assuming lack of external meaningful developments. By fixing the exchange rate to a credible currency, pegs can reduce inflation and inflation vol- atility. This “credibility channel” is central: countries effec- tively import the policy discipline of the anchor currency, which strengthens confidence, stabilizes expectations, and can support higher growth by reducing uncertainty and risk premia. In addition, stable exchange rates reduce foreign-exchange risk, facilitating trade and financial integration, while provid- ing a clear and transparent framework for policymakers. However, these benefits are not free. Maintaining a peg requires sound macroeconomic policies—often supported by prudent fiscal management. Peg credibility is typically con- tingent on a structural current account surplus (or at least a basic balance surplus) and adequate external buffers. Since its establishment in 1973, the UAE has operated a peg regime for its currency, the dirham. While the peg initially used the IMF SDR as an anchor, it transitioned toward the US dollar, with the official hard peg set at AED 3.6725 per USD since 1997—formalizing an already de facto dollar peg. The UAE clearly meets the typical prerequisites: persistent current account surpluses and sizeable foreign assets. NEETs represent the most detached segment of the labour force — people neither building skills nor adding to labour force participation. A rising NEET share implies a growing pool of structurally disengaged workers. Why is this important? A rising NEET population worsens long-run matching efficiency (think skills atrophy, employer reluctance to hire). Put simply, today's NEETs are tomorrow's hard-to-employ working population. That said, this is a very narrow measure of mismatch. Looking at the NEETs population won't capture mismtach in prime-age or older cohorts, which dominate wage-setting. It also conflates very different groups (short-term frictional vs. long-term disengaged). The bad news is that the NEETs population has risen, and as of Q1-26 sits at 13.5% (of the relevant population group). This marks its highest level since 2013. The increase in NEETs may be a byproduct of lower vacancies and/or skills/geographic mismatches. If unemployed, this would also widen the pool of available candidates seeking employment – adding to a looser labour market. A pure unemployment rate misses people who have jobs but want more hours (underemployed) or are working more than preferred (overemployed). The under-over employment ratio therefore captures hours mismatch — a dimension of labour market friction that wage data alone won't show. Rising underemployment relative to overemployment suggests that workers may have less bargaining power, accepting suboptimal hours. Why look at the under/over employment rate gap? Simply, this captures a qualitative dimension of mismatch that may be missed by just looking at the headline unemployment rate data. This may also be particularly relevant in the post- pandemic period as part-time and gig work jumped. A rising ratio is a direct constraint on wage demands – workers can't quit if they are increasingly looking for more hours. Where is the underemployment-overemployment rate gap? On our estimates this is trending higher – as we would expect. As of March 2026, this sits at -0.96 – well above the trough of -3.3 in Q2-22. Indeed, the uptrend suggests that we are seeing a push towards a more balanced labour market where the underemployment rate is equivalent to the over-employment rate. NEET rates. These episodes often involved sharp currency depreciation or devaluation, and in some cases a re-peg at higher levels. In all of these cases, the move away from the peg was driven by a build-up of unsustainable pres- sures, fueled by twin deficits and often exacerbated by portfo- lio outflows, which pushed buffers to unsustainable levels. As a result, there are far fewer examples of a more “positive” case for a de-peg motivated by a stronger starting position— potentially more relevant to the UAE. records.text: only modestly in March (to around US$505bn from US$511bn), driven by a contrac- tion at the central bank, while bank NFA increased—pointing to a reallocation within the system rather than outright deple- tion. Similar to what has been seen across the GCC, countries reporting FX reserve data show broadly stable positions and no evidence of large-scale liquidation of external assets or gold, as volumes have remained broadly unchanged. This resilience reflects both financing choices and adjust- ments in external flows. On the financing side, GCC sover- eigns—including the UAE—have largely stayed out of the Eurobond market since the onset of the shock, instead relying more heavily on private placements and alternative funding channels to meet external financing needs. This has reduced the need to draw down official FX reserves or liquidate exter- nal assets, helping preserve NFA positions. Trade data from early reporting countries such as Qatar, Bah- rain, and Saudi Arabia confirm that the disruption is affecting both revenues and expenditures, partly offsetting pressures as we expect to also be the case in the UAE. The coexistence of weaker exports and sharply lower imports implies that, while the export shock is sizeable, the net effect on the current account is mitigated, limiting external imbalances. While uncertainty remains high, our baseline for 2026 assumes a strong recovery in the current account, contingent on the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and higher oil prices

Using a sample of 142 deals originated prior to the start of 2024 who have already reported data covering delinquency patterns in April, delinquencies have remained in line with pre-existing patterns (Exhibit 18). records.text: 1 June 2026 World Outlook Page 26 Deutsche Bank AG increase since the 1980s oil shock (excluding consumption tax hikes)—surprised well above both consensus and our own upper-bound estimates. This suggests that the cost pass-through from oil prices is behaving nonlinearly. Standard economic models, which are often linear, tend to underestimate inflation during large shocks. When cost increases surpass a certain threshold, firms are more likely to raise prices across the board. Research from the BoJ (2023) supports this, indicating that the pass-through to consumer prices accelerates when CGPI inflation exceeds roughly 2%, a threshold that has already been breached. Factoring in these dynamics, we have significantly revised up our inflation outlook. While headline CPI will be volatile due to potential government price control measures, we expect core-core CPI (excluding fresh food and energy) to accelerate from July 2026, peaking at around 3.5% in early 2027 before decelerating towards 2%. This view is materially above our previous forecast and higher than the market consensus. records.text: iew, but only over time, not for this year. Core goods are roughly one-third of core CPI, and the bulk of consumer goods are imported. Domestic AI adoption would be hard pressed to lower the cost of foreign goods. Shelter inflation is about 40% of core. The rent quotes that drive this component are determined by current supply and current demand, not by productivity. Thus almost ¾ of core CPI is hard to see affected in the near term from AI productivity. Over time, turnover in the labor market could damp housing demand, overseas adoption of AI could reduce goods prices, and of course the other services components will likely benefit, although the competitive landscape of each sub-sector will determine how much. The inflation outlook is particularly opaque right now. The energy shock could prove to be persistent, and our assumptions about modest passthrough of energy into core will have to be questioned if oil prices are above $100/bbl at the end of the year. It also seems clear that AI is inflationary in the near term and only over time could it become disinflationary. With available data, however, the near-term inflationary effects look modest, though we do see upside risk. The disinflationary effect over time is more murky, and the inflation we see will be the net of many forces, including how quickly the central bank is able to stimulate the economy to take advantage of higher and rising productivity.
