records.text: Driven Demand from Life Insurers On May 21, BoJ released “International Comparison of Life Insurers: Evolving Business Models and Financial Stability Issues” (Link). The report highlights ongoing changes in the business models of life insurers—traditionally stable investors in super‑long bonds— including diversification of investment portfolios, increased use of risk transfer, and shifts in product offerings. Specifically, the report notes that the prolonged low interest rate environment prior to the COVID‑19 pandemic led to a decline in assumed rates, reducing the attractiveness of sav- ings‑oriented products. As a result, there has been a shift away from guaranteed‑return prod- ucts toward more investment‑oriented products, such as unit‑linked products, which com- bine insurance protection with investment components linked to the performance of underlying assets. Such changes in product composition imply a shortening of liability duration. As liabilities become less long‑dated, this in turn suggests a structural decline in demand for super‑long bonds from an ALM perspective. From an international perspective, Japan and Germany—where savings‑type products with long contractual maturities have historically been prevalent—tend to have relatively long liability durations, exceeding 10 years. In our baseline, with the Strait of Hormuz open by end-June, the energy shock is expected to reduce 2026 GDP growth from 1.1% to 0.5%. In an adverse scenario, with the Strait closed until summer's end, 2026 GDP growth could fall to zero, implying an outright recession. HICP inflation would be higher at 3.5% in 2026 but not necessarily stronger in 2027 due to lower growth (2.5%). Lower growth might still warrant 'measured' monetary tightening despite higher inflation. Uncertainty bands around macro forecasts are wider in the alternative scenario. Non-linear effects are more likely, increasing downside risks to growth: job losses, deleveraging, and fuel shortages (diesel shortages being more detrimental than jet fuel). If the Strait of Hormuz opens earlier (early June), the 0.5% growth forecast for 2026 would mostly hold. Growth would improve from Q3 instead of Q4, largely boosting the 2027 forecast back to pre-conflict levels (1.3%) or slightly higher. 'Measured' monetary tightening would still be appropriate for risk management. Upside risks. Faster growth drivers include a quicker peace deal and declining energy prices, more fiscal easing, resilient global growth and exports (e.g., from rising Chinese imports), and increased AI spending in Europe. Fed Watcher Fed Watcher Date 1 June 2026 Hawks on hold...for now The balance of Fed communications over the past week remained hawkish, with officials emphasizing salient upside inflation risks alongside a still resilient labor market. While most participants continued to frame policy as near neutral and well positioned, the persistence of inflation —alongside tariff and energy shocks — pushed the distribution of views towards greater optionality, including explicit willingness by many officials to consider rate hikes if disinflation fails to resume, such as Governor Cook, St. Louis Fed’s Musalem and Minneapolis Fed’s Kashkari. That said, officials stopped short of calling for rate hikes as a baseline outcome. On the dovish side, Governor Bowman continued to argue for looking through temporarily elevated inflation driven by energy, arguing that underlying inflation remains only somewhat above target. While she remained close to the dovish end of the Committee, she acknowledged that progress on inflation has stalled and is thus open to reassess the balance of risks if the energy shocks persisted. Cyclical vs. structural labor market issues Also this week, External Deputy Governor Nicholas Vincent spoke on the labor market, noting that low turnover and high long-term unemployment, particularly among young workers, could be due to structural factors such as deteriorating demo- graphics, skills mismatches and the rise of AI, rather than simply weak growth and elevated uncertainty. He also stressed that easing policy when structural factors are more prominent than cyclical ones could be a mistake, stoking inflation and arguably delaying the needed restructuring. This point strikes us as debatable: structural adjustment invariably brings with it frictions that policy support can help smooth. But his sentiment continues a recent string of mod- estly hawkish comments from Governing Council members. While we acknowledge that this communication may be tell- ing us something about the Governing Council’s reaction function, it also may simply be a form of "cheap talk" given muted core inflation and stable inflation expectations. • Canada slips into technical recession as 1Q GDP falls • 2026 Financial Stability Report points to resilience but highlights rising vulnerabilities amid trade, oil shocks • Speech by BOC’s Vincent flagged labor market issues as potentially more structural than cyclical GDP growth declined for a second consecutiv

Overall, we see quarterly GDP growth running at just around 0.1% q-o-q for the remainder of the year, taking annual GDP growth to 1%. We expect falling energy prices and political uncertainty to boost GDP growth again around the turn of the year, leaving output expanding by 1.2% in 2027. We expect GDP growth to jump to 1.6% in 2028. Risks to our projections are skewed to the downside. Indeed, higher oil prices and a broadening of inflationary pressures could hit sentiment and spending faster than pencilled in with real disposable incomes squeezed by more than projected. Labour Market : The UK labour market remains weak. After a very short lived rebound to start the year, hiring plans have levelled off. The jobless rate in March pushed back to 5%. The underemployment rate is higher at around 8.5%. And the share of marginally attached workers in the labour market sits at a cyclical high of 22.5%. Labour flow data underscore the weak labour market state: job churn is back to below-normal levels and the UK quits rate has receded meaningfully. Higher frequency data remain markedly weak too with job vacancies down to their lowest level in six years. Elevated domestic and geopolitical uncertainty will do very little to quench business concerns. We expect the jobless rate to peak at 5.4% in late summer. The NIR target of a minimum US$8 billion cumulative increase in 2026 represents the single most consequential quantitative threshold. IMF staff explicitly noted that condi- tions are in place for NIR to exceed this target, and that the authorities have been encouraged to “accelerate reserve pur- chases and deliver on their ambition of exceeding this year's NIR target.” The program is designed to front-load reserve accumulation precisely because of the 2027 debt wall. Every dollar accumulated in 2026 is a dollar less of vulnerability heading into election year. The year 2027 is the single most consequential risk horizon in the Argentina program, and it was referenced explicitly in the IMF staff report more than 20 times. Banxico’s most recent bond operation (buying back short-tenor paper while selling longer tenors, switch date 29 May) adds supply of Mbonos but does not appear to pose any structural risk to local bonds, we argue. Rather, it simply offers a better level to capture a potential spread compression. Our analysis of 10 such switches since January 2025 shows that the 10y Mbonos asset swap spread widened by a median 2bp in the week preceding each switch. The government is currently using the FY25 contingency reserve to fund subsidies and keep gasoline prices capped at JPY170. If the current subsidy level were to continue, including JPY41.8/liter for gasoline, the budget would likely be exhausted by end-June, making a budget increase only a matter of time. If the full amount of the newly created contingency reserve were allocated to these subsidies, payments could continue through year-end at the current subsidy level (Figure 2). That said, depending on oil price developments, higher subsidy amounts may become necessary, leaving a risk that the budget could still be exhausted around autumn. Within the government and ruling coalition, there is a view that the gasoline subsidy program, which costs around JPY400bn-500bn per month, should be scaled back12 . Referring to a ruling coalition proposal that gasoline subsidies should be handled flexibly with sustainability in mind, the PM said that “the government will proceed with the necessary review, ” appearing to leave room for changes to the gasoline price cap. While this represents a significant acceleration, we believe the current shock lacks the self-sustaining characteristics of the previous energy crisis. The key difference is the underlying state of the economy: softer domestic demand and a loosening labor market will limit the pass-through to core prices and reduce the risk of a wage-price spiral. While the government has so far refrained from large-scale, price-containing measures – in contrast to four years ago – this also means demand is not being artificially propped up. Nevertheless, risks are clearly tilted to the upside, with a potential tipping point during the summer months when demand for transport fuel peaks. Still, our core view remains that while inflation will accelerate, it is unlikely to become as entrenched as it did in the last cycle. Public finances – The pressure is mounting on the 2027 deficit. We forecast the French public deficit will reach 5.2% of GDP in 2026 and rise to 5.4% in 2027. While near-term discipline should keep the 2026 deficit close to its target, this apparent stability masks some underlying deterioration. The primary risk is not a cyclical downturn this year, but rather the structural embedding of the current inflation shock into the 2027 budget. Against this backdrop, China’s high-speed rail network is often faster, cheaper, and increasingly the default choice for domestic travel. In effect, some of the jet fuel demand may now be shifting to the power grid via electrified rail, rather than disappearing altogether. Taken together, developments in China and Europe raise a larger set of questions: how much of today’s demand weakness is likely to reverse once conditions normalize, and how much reflects a more durable shift in consumption? Put differently, could the world actually function with something like 9% less oil? The answer is nuanced. A decline of that magnitude would typically read as recessionary—especially when set against the Global Financial Crisis, when the world’s oil demand fell by only about 2% at its trough. But if a meaningful share of the reduction comes from substitution rather than forgone activity, the macro signal is materially different. Consider the mechanics. Despite the relative calm in broader markets, the physical supply shock itself has been immense. Supply losses linked to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz were severe and intensified further after the US blockade effectively halted Iranian oil exports. records.text: 1 June 2026 World Outlook Deutsche Bank AG Page 15 Euro Area Summary: Before the energy shock, Europe's macro outlook was a "two-economy problem": domestic cyclical resilience in 2025, boosted by German fiscal spending in 2026, contrasted with a medium-term outlook clouded by weak competitiveness and lack of strategic autonomy. The stagflationary energy shock, anticipated monetary tightening, and a weaker-than-expected German fiscal multiplier have worsened the near-term outlook. Growth. Since December, we've lowered the euro area GDP forecast for 2026 to 0.5% (from 1.1%), largely due to the Middle East crisis and energy shock, alongside a weaker German fiscal multiplier. The energy shock impacts through several channels: a real income shock to consumption from higher inflation, increased uncertainty leading to lower investment and higher savings, tighter monetary policy, and reduced exports from lower global growth. This forecast assumes the Strait of Hormuz opens by mid-year, with Brent crude averaging USD93/bbl in 2026 and USD80/bbl in 2027. A more immediate reopening of the Strait would leave the 2026 GDP growth forecast at 0.5%. Either way, we would forecast a -0.1% qoq contraction in Q2 GDP, consistent with current trackers. Our baseline has no growth in Q3; faster reopening could nudge this up to 0.1% qoq. This suggests an economy near a technical recession this summer. records.text: CHF: Stairway to haven. Over the past two months we have argued that the n repercussions of the energy shock should apply steady downward pressure on EUR/CHF. The Franc’s safe-haven properties are particularly relevant in geopolitical, inflationary, and downside European growth shocks, and the ongoing conflict has elements of all three. The shift in the SNB’s intervention bias meanwhile has been key in capping any haven-based gains for the Franc so far, but we think a reacceleration in domestic Swiss inflation should be enough to shift that bias back to a neutral setting and uncover those haven benefits. This is the main angle through which we will be watching the SNB’s upcoming meeting on June 18, with headline CPI already running above the Bank’s most recent Q2 projection, and consensus expecting a further increase in next week’s May report. This path to looser SNB FX management is central to our expectation for further CHF outperformance in the months ahead, but several important risks remain. First and foremost, EUR/CHF carry-to-vol is close to post-2015 highs, weakening risk-reward in outright downside positions. Second, we find evidence that gold’s shifting correlation to risk is spilling over to the Franc and is likely to continue to be a source of idiosyncratic vol for the Franc via its terms of trade linkages. records.text: Ning Sun 1 June 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Brazil – Limited monetary easing, positive BRL We recently visited Brazil and met with policymakers, local banks, political consultants, and investors to reassess our constructive view on BRL. Ahead of the trip, BRL already stood out as our preferred high -carry trade suggestion, supported by a strong external position and Brazil’s status as an energy exporter. The central question was whether the Central Bank of Brazil (BCB) would maintain policy tightness , and therefore preserve BRL’s carry appeal. Based on our discussions, the answer is yes. Despite e levated political noise and limited fiscal progress, the macro policy mix continues to support our positive view on BRL. We treat the recent weakness as buying opportunity. Fiscal policy - progress made but credibility remains low . Brazil’s fiscal position has improved meaningfully since the pandemic, with the primary deficit narrowing to below 1% of GDP (Figure 1) , well below the broader EM average. However, the debt trajectory remains challenging. High nominal financing costs (around 12 –13% according to the Debt Management Office) combined with moderate inflation expectations (~5%) and low growth potential (~2%) imply that a primary surplus of roughly 4% of GDP would be required to stabilize debt. Although this report is not very optimistic, it is still more positive than the record lows reported by the university of Michigan. Why the divergence? The Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index is more closely tied to labor market conditions, which have remained in a “low-hire, low-fire” equilibrium. This contrasts with the University of Michigan data, which is more closely tied to consumers personal finances. In general, the consumer confidence index is a better measure of big-ticket purchases with long-payoff periods such as housing, while the sentiment indicators are a better indicator of general consumer spending. While weak consumer sentiment can be driven by multiple factors, the Philadelphia Fed’s Labor, Income, Finances, and Expectations (LIFE) survey queries respondents with a focus on their financial situation, much like the University of Michigan survey. The LIFE survey gathers information from roughly 5,000 individuals each quarter, with the first survey conducted in January 2023. The most recent survey for April 2026 was conducted between March 27th and April 9th, covering a period where national gasoline prices averaged over $4 a gallon. records.text: The ongoing convergence between (population-weighted) poor and rich economies implies that the incomes of EM economies will gradually move closer to those of developed economies – resulting in a further reduction in global income inequality – and that the share of global GDP represented by emerging markets will continue to increase over time. Looking forward, there are both positive and negative risks to long-term economic growth and convergence. The development of AI seems likely to bolster the strong performance of the US and parts of South-East Asia and lift global GDP productivity growth more generally.9 In terms of AI-related capital expenditure, South Korea and Taiwan are already the main beneficiaries, while from a development and adoption standpoint, China seems well-placed to gain. On the downside, we consider two risks especially significant: First, although global growth and trade have so far been surprisingly resilient to rising tariffs, increased protectionism could still trigger a reversal of globalization. Second, climate change represents a particular threat to Southern Asia and parts of Africa. records.text: Going forward, we expect year-over-year real income growth to pick up slightly from its current pace as policy-related distortions fade. But we continue to expect higher energy prices to erode household spending power, and we forecast only 0.9% real income growth in 2026 on a Q4/Q4 basis. Higher energy prices will likely exert a particularly large drag on income growth for lower-income households, who spend a larger share of their budget on food and energy. The slowdown in income has not translated into slower spending yet, likely because larger-than-usual tax refunds have boosted consumer cashflow since the start of the year (Exhibit 4). But as the effect of the tax cuts fades, we expect real consumer cashflow growth to slow even more significantly, to only 0.3% year-over-year by 2026Q4. The combination of slower income growth with still-strong spending growth has resulted in a decline in the saving rate to only 2.6% in April. We think that the current saving rate is likely understated by a bit under 1pp because of measurement issues with interest payments in the national accounts, but even a 3½% saving rate would be the lowest level on record outside of the pre-GFC period and 2022. While it is normal for the saving rate to be low when household wealth is very high, we expect it to normalize a bit going forward, as spending growth decelerates in response to slower income gains. records.text: ontech IP Debate around Taiwan’s outlook centers on the duration of the AI upcycle and the impact from the energy shock. Recent US hyperscaler results suggest the AI capex cycle remains intact, with strong backlogs pointing to multi-year demand that should continue to support Taiwan’s tech manufacturers. On energy, the Ministry of Economic Affairs reports June– July supplies are secured, with ample crude and gas invento- ries, while alternative Middle East routes and higher US imports are keeping shipments on track. Petrochemicals faced more pressure, but downstream spillovers appear manageable so far. Hong Kong: exports firmed, led by Asia Headline exports rose for the eighth consecutive month, up 5.0%m/m sa, lifting the annual rate to 42.9%oya. Shipments to Asia (excluding China) showed strong momentum (+5.7%m/m sa), while exports to mainland China rose for the sixth consecutive month (+2.9%), reflecting Hong Kong’s role as a re-export hub in the regional tech supply chain (Fig- ure 4). Imports firmed further on a 2.6%m/m rise, with the annual growth reaching a multi-year high at 44.4%oya. Hong Kong’s 1Q GDP reached a five-year high driven by investment (esp. inventories), while net trade was a drag as imports outpaced exports. Looking ahead, net export contri- butions may remain volatile, but strong regional tech trade and resilient mainland China exports should provide some support. What’s priced for the week ahead?: Friday’s NFP is the macro event in focus this week, kicking off a busy month of catalysts with visible kinks on the SPX surface for CPI (10th) and FOMC (17th). We continue to like IWM optionality to express macro views, particularly short-term upside gamma. A retracement in rates or geopolitical tailwind could see a short, sharper rally in IWM given its underperformance to other US indices. On the micro calendar, there are no shortage of events either in June, with a string of tech earnings this week including AVGO, ORCL, and ADBE. SpaceX is rumored to IPO the week after (June 12th), with MU reporting earnings (24th) at the end of the month. Trading exuberance: For chasing upside, we continue to like both XLK and IGV as momentum trades. In XLK, ETF composition has now grown >50% Semis. Versus history XLK implieds are less elevated than SMH. Evidenced by the software squeeze at the end of last week, IGV was underowned and we see as a potential retail target as they move down the AI risk curve. SMH remains our preferred left tail to own, given the extent of the rally (80% off March lows) and short gamma present in the sector. In QQQ and mega-cap single names, we’d consider carefully utilizing flat up-skew to trade call ratios and up and out calls.

records.text: Although USD/CAD tends to rise when trade tensions escalate, we find markets price limited trade-specific premium beyond standard cyclical drivers in our GSBEER models. During the NAFTA renegotiation, pockets of trade premium emerged around key events, but USD/CAD otherwise remained broadly in line with fundamentals (Exhibit 4). Similarly, during the 2025 fentanyl-related tariffs and Liberation Day uncertainty, the moves in USD/CAD were largely explained by rate differentials (Exhibit 5). We attribute this limited premium to the BoC’s incorporation of trade policy uncertainty—and consequent adverse impacts on activity—into its reaction function, both in 2018 and more recently. For example, in April 2018 the BoC noted that “interest rates may need to remain below the neutral range until… uncertainty around trade conflicts…has dissipated.” More recently, the April statement highlighted that new trade restrictions could warrant further easing to support economic growth. Despite hikes priced, our economists note that the hurdle remains high for the BoC to adjust the policy rate in the face of heightened trade policy uncertainty, underpinning their expectation for the BoC to remain on hold through 2026. In this way, trade shocks more durably impact the USD/CAD via rate differentials, rather than as a sustained premium over traditional cyclical drivers. records.text: We are not the first to adjust for population size in this way. Previous studies have also weighted by population size and, consistent with our findings, have found stronger evidence of convergence on this basis.7 Nonetheless, those studies maintain that, when assessing which economic policies drive growth and convergence, it is still reasonable to treat each country as an equal unit, since such policies are largely determined at the national level. We disagree for two reasons: First, economic welfare is a study of people, not nations, and if more people reside in some nations than others, they should be weighted accordingly. Second, a country’s size is itself a potentially significant factor influencing growth and convergence. If larger countries tend to grow faster than smaller ones, this may partially be attributable to their size. Overlooking this aspect risks missing a potentially important determinant of growth.8 The contrast that we find with unweighted convergence studies suggests an important and intuitive point: periods of rapid globalization, such as 2000-10, tend to be particularly beneficial for the development of small economies with limited domestic markets. However, for large emerging market economies, economic convergence appears to be more resilient to the pace of globalization. records.text: Euro Area Outlook ECB walking the credibility-growth line Despite signs of softer economic momentum, the case for ECB policy tightening at the June meeting is firming, as headline inflation continues to edge higher and incoming data point to building pipeline price pressures. We continue to expect 25bp hikes at the June and September meetings. • The Middle East conflict and higher energy prices are clearly weighing on euro area activity. Our GDP tracker still points to about 0.1% q/q growth in Q2, but survey-based nowcasts based on PMIs and EC indicators flag downside risks, with stagnation or a mild contraction increasingly plausible. • Our forecast is for headline inflation to have risen to 3.3% y/y in May, with core re-accelerating to 2.4% y/y. Firms’ pricing intentions remain strong in surveys, while PPI data from France, Italy and Spain suggest mounting pipeline pressures, particularly upstream. • ECB communication increasingly points to the need for tightening, making a 25bp hike in June all but locked in, even if a near-term US Iran agreement were to materialise. Beyond June, we continue to see the broadening of inflation pressures as consistent with at least one additional 25bp hike in September. From diverging growth paths pre-conflict... However, as these pressures persist, we expect a greater share of the adjustment to shift to inflation-adjusted spending. An alternative interpretation is that the low saving rate reflects wealth effects, as households internalize future gains in productivity and purchasing power from AI. While we see this as part of the explanation for why the saving rate has remained below pre-pandemic norms (6–8%) throughout this expansion, we are skeptical that such effects have intensified materially in recent months. That said, this represents an upside risk to our outlook, and, if realized, could provide one possible trigger for Fed hikes over the medium term (see Federal Reserve Commentary: What would trigger a 2026 Fed hike?). Lean inventories downplay recession risks and amplify inflation risks Although we are wary of inventory measurement, we do note that downward revisions to inventory investment in the second GDP estimates make stocks appear even leaner in relation to sales. Indeed, a variety of BEA metrics (Figure 5) show that—on an aggregate basis—inflation- adjusted stocks are generally at or below readings seen amid the acute shortages during the post-pandemic period. records.text: ecast is broadly consistent with the BoJ's April Outlook Report, but we expect inflation to peak in the first half of 2027 and then decelerate toward 2%. A risk scenario would be a case where inflation of 3% or higher persists for a longer period. The potential triggers for this would be a further acceleration in wage growth and a delay in BoJ rate hikes (for details, please see our report "Will history repeat itself? Ueda's speech and the policy outlook"). Monetary policy: Quarterly hikes to 1.75% Sharply raising the terminal rate and pace of hikes Our February forecast, predicated on core-core CPI inflation settling around 2%, was for two 0.25% rate hikes in July 2026 and January 2027, with the policy rate then holding at 1.25%. However, with a significant oil price surge making an inflation overshoot unavoidable, and with the associated risk of private-sector inflation expectations becoming unanchored or destabilized, this policy rate forecast is no longer appropriate. In this forecast revision, we expect the policy rate to be raised to 1.75%. This is near the midpoint of the BoJ's estimated neutral rate band (1.1% to 2.5%). With inflation set to exceed its target, a restrictive monetary policy stance—with a policy rate above the neutral rate, or at least in the upper half of the neutral band (1.75-2.5%)— would theoretically be desirable. However, for large emerging market economies – especially those in East Asia – economic convergence appears relatively robust. This ongoing convergence implies that the share of global GDP represented by emerging markets (and East Asian EMs in particular) will continue to rise over time. Looking ahead, risks exist in both directions. The development of AI seems likely n to bolster the strong performance of the US and parts of East Asia (in particular, China, South Korea and Taiwan). records.text: We update our AI adoption tracker through May 2026. n AI-related investment growth remains strong, particularly for semiconductors, n where equity analysts expect global revenue growth of 57% from current levels by the end of 2026. AI-related investment in the US national accounts also continues to rise and now stands at $384bn (1.2% of GDP) above its 2022 level. AI-related hardware shipments from Asia remain elevated and US AI hardware net imports surged to $52bn in March. AI adoption by firms ticked down by 0.3pp to 19.5% among US establishments n (with adoption expected to rise to 22.7% in the next 6 months) according to the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS). Company management, information services, and professional services firms continue to lead adoption. At a detailed subsector level, computing, publishing, and web hosting firms report adoption levels at or exceeding 50%, and chemical manufacturing firms report the largest expected increase in adoption over the next 6 months. Establishments with over 250 employees continue to lead in adoption (36.1%), but medium-sized firms with 100-250 employees are catching up (30.6%). Other business surveys note that many firms are beginning to experiment with agentic AI systems. AI’s labor market impact remains visible but narrow. records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 01/06/2026 18:08:05 GMT Distributed on: 01/06/2026 18:08:05 GMT 1 June 2026 Deutsche Bank Research Europe Economics Focus Europe Date WO Forecast Update: An unavoidable shock This publication contains the European sections from the latest Deutsche Bank World Outlook published on 1 June 2026 and includes additional sections on France and Italy. Euro area: The euro area faces a significant economic slowdown in 2026. On account of the Middle East energy shock we have downgraded growth to 0.5% from 1.1% in our November World Outlook (WO). A US-Iran deal is expected in June, with Brent oil to fall to USD86/bbl in Q4 and USD80/bbl in 2027. We expect a small contraction in Q2 GDP, a gradual recovery to begin in the second half, and output to expand 1.1% in 2027. Relative to the last WO, inflation is significantly faster. HICP is expected to be 3.1% in 2026 and still well above target at 2.5% in 2027. Core HICP is expected to be 2.4% in both years, indicating persistent underlying price pressures. In turn, we expect the ECB to implement a "measured" tightening, hiking policy rates twice to 2.50% in summer 2026. Germany: The Middle East conflict has presented the German economy with multifaceted headwinds. Growth momentum is therefore likely to weaken towards the middle of the year. First, to use it as funding, it is necessary to generate a surplus in the Foreign Exchange Fund Special Account, of which up to 70% can be transferred to the general account in the following fiscal year. This surplus is the difference between revenue and expenditure calculated in accordance with laws and regulations. Foreign exchange valuation gains corresponding to unrealized gains are not included in revenue, while foreign exchange trading gains corresponding to realized profits are booked as revenue. In addition, the JPY obtained through intervention is used for redemption of financing bills, but this is not counted as expenditure. In other words, if the sale of foreign bonds can increase trading gains, it could become a funding source through the surplus. However, the issue lies in how those trading gains are calculated. In fact, under the legal framework, when foreign bonds are sold, trading gains are only the difference between the sale amount and the JPY-converted amount of those bonds using the average FX rate from two months earlier (Figure 6). In other words, from the perspective of FX movements, trading gains are affected only by the past two months. Meanwhile, the JPY increase generated by JPY depreciation up to two months earlier becomes a valuation gain and is reflected only on the balance sheet of the Foreign Exchange Fund Special Account. However, the US could still play a key role, using its strong leverage to try to smooth the process and reach a negotiated solution, but recent US signals arguably point to an extension rather than a compression of the transition timeline. While the US is still working under Secretary Rubio's three-stage plan, which contemplates a transition, there seems to be at least a mismatch in timelines (see Venezuela: Too much, too soon?). The opposition’s urgency contrasts with the US administration’s preference for sequencing economic stabilization first. This generates uncertainty about the speed and magnitude of the economic recovery. We remain of the view that in order for the economy to achieve its full potential and reach the most optimistic scenarios of recovery values for the debt in a potential restructuring process a political transition is necessary. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 01 Jun 2026 10:53:56 ET │ 13 pages US Economics Inflation Weekly – “Cleaner” shelter inflation ahead CITI'S TAKE Core PCE rose 0.24%MoM in April, slightly softer than the 0.26% increase we had been penciling in, but with revisions higher to PCE in February keeping annual core PCE above 3%, at 3.3%YoY. Core goods prices in PCE continue to run stronger than in CPI due to inappropriately-measured computer software and accessories prices. “Supercore” PCE was soft in April but will be boosted by rebounding portfolio management fees in May. Housing inflation in PCE was stronger, reflecting the same “catch-up” issue as rents/OER in April CPI. After April, data will again give a “cleaner” read on the monthly and annual pace of shelter inflation, as shutdown-related measurement issues have corrected. Case Shiller home prices continued to slow in March, rising less than 1%YoY. We continue to think these leading signals will mean further slowing in shelter inflation in coming months. This is likely to raise the hurdle for subsequent rate hikes. In summary, we expect the BoJ to continue hiking rates quarterly from July 2026, with the policy rate reaching 1.75% by April 2027. If risk scenarios, such as a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, materialize and oil prices remain high, a larger magnitude of rate hikes would be necessary. In particular, if the Fed re-enters a hiking cycle, the BoJ's hiking pace could be faster and the terminal rate higher. Until now, the basic stance of BoJ policy board members has been to raise rates gradually in response to economic and price developments, rather than aiming for a specific interest rate level. However, a speech by board member Masu in May stated, "To complete the normalization of monetary policy in Japan, I am convinced that the Bank needs to raise the policy interest rate further, so that it falls solidly within the estimated range of the neutral interest rate, thereby ensuring the flexibility needed to swiftly adjust the policy rate in either direction, depending on economic conditions." records.text: s path. • Fuel oil demand destruction is estimated at 600 kbd so far, driven by weaker shipping and industrial activity, refinery disruptions, and lower oil-fired power burn. Unlike jet fuel, a meaningful share of this loss may not return even after crude flows normalize, because end users are adapting in ways that tend to persist. In shipping, higher bunker costs are accelerating slow steaming, route optimization, and fleet-efficiency upgrades. In power, governments are minimizing oil burn through conservation, grid optimization, faster renewable deployment, and in some cases greater coal use. In industry, firms are tightening processes, selectively electrifying systems, and reducing energy intensity (Figure 7). A relevant precedent is global shipping after the 2008 financial crisis and the IMO 2020 transition. Slow steaming began as a temporary response to higher costs, but became embedded as operators found they could materially cut fuel use with limited impact on supply chains, evolving into a structurally more fuel-efficient operating model for parts of the fleet (Figure 8). Because fuel oil is relatively easy to replace at the margin, even a partial step-down can become structural. The implication is an incomplete recovery and a faster long-term decline in fuel oil demand even once conditions stabilize. House Rules The FY27 Budget unveiled the most significant change in taxation of capital since the late 1990s. Subject to (not guar- anteed) passage through the Senate, the government plans to eliminate the current 50% capital gains tax discount (a halv- ing of the marginal tax rate, for assets held for more than one year), moving to an inflation indexation approach. This will tax gains on assets above inflation, at the maximum of one’s marginal tax rate, and 30%. The changes, originally mooted to address property speculation, will also apply to equity wealth and returns on other forms of business ownership. The government plans to simultaneously remove negative gearing of investor housing on existing dwellings. Negative gearing is the right to deduct net rental losses – i.e. when interest and related costs exceed rental income – against other forms of taxable income. In our view, adding a causality measure provides deeper insight into FX dynamics as it allows us to assess whether the variables that appear to be driving FX also contain leading information. How does FEFA fit within our framework? Others in our suite of FX models, such as BNP Paribas STEER and BNP Paribas CLEER , use a defined set of variables. STEER and CLEER allow for the relationship between FX and the explanatory variables to change over time (i.e. dynamic coefficients), but the explanatory variables themselves remain the same (i.e. static explanatory variables). FEFA allows for increased flexibility, given its ability to capture changes in the explanatory variables themselves over time. As with all our FX quantitative models, we will consider FEFA as an input into our macro discretionary views and trade ideas, rather than a stand-alone systematic trading model. FEFA enables us to precisely understand at a given point in time the cross-asset market variables to which our FX views and trade ideas are exposed. It complements our other FX valuation quant models, as it enables us to combine our outlook for the variables that are driving FX with current valuations to give a better indication of the chances of spot converging with its fair value. records.text: 1 June 2026 World Outlook Deutsche Bank AG Page 11 United States Summary: We remain constructive on the US growth outlook, with only a small downward revision since our last World Outlook, as fiscal policy, accommodative financial conditions, and AI investment counterbalance higher oil prices. Resilient growth should reinforce recent stabilization in the labor market this year, but inflation remains stubbornly high, and its drivers look more worrying to us. While our baseline remains that the Fed is on hold indefinitely, there are increasing risks that rate hikes might be needed to put inflation on a more sustainable path towards 2%. Growth: We continue to see a resilient US growth backdrop with tailwinds from fiscal policy, accommodative financial conditions, and AI-related investment counterbalancing headwinds from higher oil prices. On net, we have modestly lowered our growth forecast this year, with Q4/Q4 and annual/annual real GDP growth now projected at 2.2% (down from 2.3% previously). Higher oil prices will weigh on disposable income and consumer spending, which we now expect to grow only 1.9% this year, and 1.75% over the back half of 2026. Further out, we expect growth to remain above 2%, with robust productivity continuing to power the US economy over the medium term. On the second issue, Moody's Ratings downgraded Mexico's long-term debt rating by one notch to Baa3, from Baa2, last week. While this was anticipated, as Moody's set its outlook to Negative, from Stable back in November 2024, it came on top of the unexpected S&P Global outlook revision to Negative from Stable, just a week earlier. Both rating agencies mentioned that the rationale behind their decisions were based on slow growth, with no grounds to anticipate a better outlook for economic activity in the medium term, and fiscal trends. On the latter, they highlighted the upward trend of the debt-to-GDP ratio, despite the recent consolidation efforts, as well as lower margins to react amid shocks. The three major issues that are reducing the government's fiscal flexibility are Pemex's poor operational results, despite significant government financial support and the likely continued need for it, elevated social programs at the constitutional level, and more recently the modification of the precedence of infrastructure spending, right after financial costs and the budgets of autonomous institutions. As a result, it is going to be more difficult for the government to cut back spending on these two categories in case of a shock. In the two most recent Mbonos coupon events (5 March 2026, 4 December 2025), the 10y asset swap spread first tightened by roughly 5bp on average in the two weeks leading up to each payment, and then narrowed by another 12bp in the two weeks following the payment (Figure 2). If a similar flow of funds into Mbonos occurs around the June 4 coupon payment, we anticipate a comparable compression of the asset swap spread. Middle East deal still the key risk: A Middle East peace accord is a risk, as this could trigger a renewed rally in global fixed income (ASW widening). However, we see this risk as contained because TIIE-F has recovered a third of its initial losses, while the bond market has trailed. Consequently, even if a deal materialises, TIIE-F has limited room to rally further relative to bonds, curbing potential for additional spread widening. Based on the historical pattern, we expect the Mbonos asset swap spread to narrow after the government’s latest debt-switching activity. records.text: omplete normalization has yet to pan out. The credit rating upgrade from Fitch, to B−, reflects a genuine improvement in fundamentals. But the IMF’s second review is also a reminder that the pro- gram has not yet cleared its hardest test. Reserve coverage remains well below adequacy benchmarks. A US$30 billion debt service obligation arrives in 2027 at the most challeng- ing moment when political incentives to loosen fiscal and monetary policy will be at their strongest. The program's institutional architecture, by design, is most relaxed at the most demanding moment. The key variable to watch is not the fiscal surplus, in our view. Milei has demonstrated his commitment there. It is whether the BCRA can accumulate sufficient NIR in 2026 to build a buffer against the inevitable 2027 turbulence. In other words, to build the anti-fragility we called for following the mid-term elections. The program targets US$8 billion mini- mum in NIR accumulation this year. Market participants should watch whether Argentina exceeds that target. Every dollar above US$8 billion is insurance against a scenario in which political pressure, market volatility, and a massive debt wall collide simultaneously in Argentina's presidential elec- tion year. Bonds: Early on in my trip, nearly every client wanted to know the risk posed by rising bonds yields but once bond yields rallied a bit (on a falling oil price) this concern seems to have evaporated. We think it will return. We continue to see the structural risk that governments will spend until bond yields discipline them not to. The bonds to equities relationship is highly unstable (in Japan, for example, the 10 year bond yields early on in my career was 10x the dividend yield, while at the trough on the Topix the dividend yield was 3x bond yields—a roughly 15-fold swing). We think the best indicator of rising risk associated with rising bond yields is if rising bond yields are accompanied by wider credit spreads or if inflation expectations in the bond market challenge the central bank’s credibility (which would then force the Fed to be more aggressive). Administrative complexity Simpler structures generally reduce the surface area for operational fail- ure. Where structures are inherently complex, mitigants include overcollat- eralization such as a minimum 103% asset-to-debt ratio, conservative investment earnings assumptions such as 0% on certain investments, and cash flow projections demonstrat- ing positive net revenue each interest period. Administrative errors by trustees, ser- vicers, and other transaction parties can translate into missed transfers, misapplied funds, or delayed draws. Flow of funds The key focus is a clearly defined pri- ority of payments in both routine and default scenarios, a transparent and sustainable fee framework, and prompt investment of receipts in per- mitted investments consistent with liquidity needs. A strong guarantee does not eliminate the risk that funds are trapped, subor- dinated to fees, or redirected to non- debt service purposes. records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 29/05/2026 15:22:11 GMT Distributed on: 29/05/2026 15:22:11 GMT 29 May 2026 Deutsche Bank Research Europe United Kingdom Economics UK Weekly Digest Date Who's matching? Labour market mismatches back at cyclical lows Last week we published our first quarterly labour market chartbook highlighting the state of the labour market. The broad gist: the labour market was on an uncomfortable trajectory – and that's likely before even taking into account some of the unfolding effects of AI (something we will discuss in the coming months). In this weekly, we look specifically at labour market matching – updating our models on how workers are able to match with existing vacancies. The combination of labour market tightness and matching indicators tells us an important labour market story. What's the main takeaway? Firms, in aggregate, are finding it much easier to match vacancies with workers in a looser labour market. There are some exceptions though (particularly for NEETs). Matching efficiency may be lower here. But ultimately, the combination of a looser labour market matters more in dampening wage bargaining power. This should spell some good news for the MPC as we enter a new inflation wave. Four measures of labour market matching No one indicator captures the totality of labour market matching – a good proxy of slack and wage bargaining power. Thus far, economic activity has largely held up in response to the energy shock, helping to shore up any downside risks to the labor market. Collectively, the balance of the week’s data will provide some insights into whether the recent firmness in business activity continues. Monday’s manufacturing ISM (54.0 vs. 52.7) as well as Thursday’s services ISM (53.9 vs. 53.6) should edge higher given recent positive momentum in regional surveys. For example, board member Masu carefully explained the need for rate hikes in his May speech: "I often hear that the combination of wage increases and policy interest rate hikes is causing difficulties for firms. It is indeed not hard to imagine the significant challenges business owners are facing in raising wages, given labor shortages and the need to comply with the increase in the minimum wage in Japan. However, if the inflation rate cannot be contained at an appropriate level, this could lead to a vicious cycle in which firms have to further raise wages to retain workers. The Bank considers that, to ensure that the wage increases firms have managed to achieve are not in vain, it is important to manage the inflation rate through appropriate monetary policy and thereby maintain real wage growth." With respect to the Bloomberg Agg sub-indices, the MBS Index OAS widened 3bp MTD to 23bp versus US IG Corp OAS which is 5bp tighter to 73bp, with this divergence accelerating by 3bp in just the last 2 weeks. The spread divergence is driven by rate vol repricing MBS extension risk and thus prepay probabilities, while US IG Corp spreads have rallied given ongoing manageable net supply and strong demand (inflows last Tuesday were yet again 17% above their 1m average despite 1m trailing returns of -1.8% vs. March outflows that emerged as 1m trailing returns hit -2.1%). The move in spreads has translated into MBS excess returns of +4bp MTD vs IG Corp excess returns of +48bp, a 44bp differential. Total returns tell a similar story: MBS returned -49bp vs IG Corp returns -15bp, partially a function of the duration on MBS extending significantly as rates go higher and thus closing the gap to corporates (currently 5.5yr for MBS vs 6.79yr for corporates). Tariff wear-off makes it unlikely Investors are pricing in two risks to the disinflation: Treasury yields remaining highly correlated with oil and AI demand pushing software and memory prices higher. Our revised targets for $IG spreads for 2H’26 are 82bps (representing a 10bps widening from current levels) and $HY spreads 305bps (representing a 44bps widening). However, concerns are more acute in €-credit, with year-end targets of 95bps for €IG (a 16bps widening from current levels) and 345bps for €HY (a 74bps widening from current levels), reflecting Europe's greater economic sensitivity and the impact of ECB tightening. If correct, this would be the widest relative value differential between €-credit & $-credit since Q4’24. EM asset classes have shown resilience, but the energy price shock has introduced significant geographical dispersion. Asia is more severely impacted due to energy import dependence, but some countries have benefited from the AI boom and China's role as a risk absorber has risen. LatAm is relatively insulated, with mixed risks across CEEMEA. Our strategists favour relative value differentiation, with a bullish bias on rates in LatAm and CEEMEA. In sum, 2026 is shaping up to be a year defined by the dual forces of technological advancement and geopolitical realignments. While the long-term outlook for productivity remains very promising, particularly in the US, the immediate future demands agile navigation through inflationary pressures and heightened volatility. So part of the steepening in the breakeven market reflects the reality that the Strait of Hormuz has now been closed for 13 weeks. The real yield curve has twist flattened, with 5-, 10-, and 30-year real yields moving by +5bp, -2bp and -10bp net of carry over the past two weeks. We believe the front- end of the curve has been anchored by hawkish Fed speak, as illustrated through the OIS curve being largely unchanged over the past two weeks. We therefore attribute the majority of the flattening to a reduction in global term premia and reduced tightening expectations ex-US. records.text: Emerging Asia Outlook The hawkish turn continues The BoK proved to be more hawkish than we expected, despite keeping its policy rate unchanged. We note the rising risk that BI could hike by 50bp instead of 25bp on 18 June to defend the IDR. By contrast, the RBI will likely stay on hold on 5 June. The hawkish turn in Emerging Asia's monetary policy cycle continued this week with the Bank of Korea (BoK). With negative terms of trade shock offset by an even stronger semiconductor export cycle, the BoK is pivoting away from the concerns around the growth downside risks, while underscoring the inflation risks. We also think the CBC's June meeting is likely to be a close call as we expect May CPI inflation to breach above 2%. Meanwhile, Sri Lanka delivered an outsized hike due to both inflation and FX concerns; we also caution against another 50bp hike from Bank Indonesia should the FX pressure continue into mid-June. Even as we expect the RBI to keep rates on hold and look through the supply shock driven inflation, we see the risk of prolonged energy price pressure creating a strong case for a 'generalised ' increase in price pressure eventually. records.text: 1 June 2026 World Outlook Deutsche Bank AG Page 35 Credit Global credit spreads have displayed remarkable resilience in the face of the twin risk factors of 1) the US/Iran War & 2) AI’s disruption of private credit markets. $IG & $HY spreads are now -6bps & -7bps tighter YTD, while being -12 & -30bps tighter than when the Iran war began on February 27. It is a similar story in Europe, where €IG & €HY spreads are flat & only +9bps wider YTD, and still -4 & -8bps tighter than pre-Iran war levels, despite Europe’s greater economic sensitivity to both higher energy prices & central bank rate hikes. Why are credit investors sanguine? Firstly, the continued influx of retail money into credit as overall yields rise are keeping credit spreads tight technically. But more fundamentally, investors believe the US/ Iran war will only lead to a temporary boost in inflation, allowing the ECB to hike less than priced and allowing the Fed to simply keep rates on hold. This coupled with limited concrete fallout from the war in terms of earnings downgrades is boosting confidence in corporate fundamentals. Lastly, US large cap corporate earnings were up +25% in Q1 as the tangible benefits of AI adoption are outweighing the fears over AI disruption . Analysis of consumer sentiment data from the University of Michigan, the Conference Board, and the Philadelphia Fed shows that even though aggregate consumer balance sheets remain resilient, consumers are somewhat pessimistic about the economy, with feelings of financial fragility intensifying in the lower income brackets. The pullback—concentrated in the Middle East and Asia—looks driven more by operational disruption than a lasting shock to mobility: airlines have rerouted flights, avoided certain Middle East refueling hubs, trimmed unprofitable routes, and run inventories more conservatively amid higher prices and elevated uncertainty. Long-haul aviation is also usually hard to substitute, particularly across Asia and on intercontinental routes. Scalable alternatives are limited, and sustainable aviation fuel remains a small, supply-constrained share of the mix. For that reason, our base case is that most of today’s jet fuel demand shortfall returns as availability normalizes. That said, higher fares and prolonged uncertainty could still leave structural fingerprints. They may accelerate the shift to remote business meetings, curb discretionary short-haul travel, and divert some passenger demand to rail where it is a viable substitute. Airlines, for their part, may prioritize profitability and load factors over rapid capacity expansion. The net result is that jet demand looks relatively resilient versus other refined products, with recovery likley, but with the key risk being a flatter long-term growth trajectory than the pre-crisis path. • Fuel oil demand destruction is estimated at 600 kbd so far, driven by weaker shipping and industrial activity, refinery disruptions, and lower oil-fired power burn. In addition, banks' net-interest margins dropped to a record low of 1.4 % in Q1, which will continue to constrain the PBoC from cutting interest rates (see China: Politburo offers no hint of additional easing, dated 29 April 2026). Consequently, if growth in May remains below 4.5 %, we expect policymakers to react by speeding up fiscal rather than lowering policy rates via monetary easing. Moreover, the July Politburo meeting could be a window for the government to announce additional fiscal stimulus if economic growth disappoints expectations. PPI reflation is not transitory: China‘s PPI inflation is more sensitive to supply rather than demand, and supply has tightened in many ways. For instance, listed companies’ capex growth has been negative since 2024, and industrial consolidation has been happening in sectors with overcapacity, notably in solar. Hence, even if energy prices fall back gradually after a permanent ceasefire later this year, we believe China‘s PPI would not fall back into deflation. PPI reflation is also driving double-digit growth in industrial corporate profits, as we observe industrial corporate profits jumping 18.2% y/y in January-April, in contrast to a mere 0.5% annual growth in 2025. As the profits of the industrial sector as a whole improve in tandem with higher PPI inflation, we believe it would eventually translate into higher wages and higher domestic demand, which is the main drag to growth.

Amid lingering uncertainty, our oil forecast assumes a re-opening of Hormuz later in June. The oil market has shown substantial flexibility in adjusting to the Iran war, but the continued disruption has led us to raise our Brent oil price forecast to USD 109/bbl in Q2. Assuming a US-Iran MOU and gradual normalization, we expect a post-conflict surplus of 4 mmb/d, leading to prices reaching USD 86/bbl in Q4 and USD 80/bbl in 2027. A deal in early June would create some optimism relative to our oil price view for Q3 but have limited impact relative to our broader macro baseline. Conversely, a more extreme downside scenario that sees the Strait of Hormuz largely closed through Q3 would push Brent crude closer to $150/bbl in Q3, turning the drag on US growth from marginal to material and pushing Europe into an outright recession. Our economists and strategists, though still largely constructive on the medium-term outlook, emphasize the non-linear risks and the broadening dispersion of economic fortunes. Expect continued volatility, as markets swing between narratives of technological triumph and stagflationary concerns. Instru- ments maturing before the 2027 presidential election carry effective yields of 5−6 percent, compared with 8−9% 2028−2029 paper, a clear term premium for political uncer- tainty. Second, the Treasury is in the process of contracting roughly US$4 billion in syndicated loans from international banks, guaranteed 40−95% by the World Bank Group, IADB, and CAF. These IFI-backed loans provide temporary bridge financing at below-market rates and are structured with grace periods of roughly three years, extending effective maturities beyond the election. Third, the BCRA has concluded repo agreements totaling US$6 billion with international banks (US$3 billion executed in January 2026 alone), providing additional FX liquidity outside the formal IMF umbrella. Finally, the financing strategy is being complemented by efforts to privatize SOEs, which are expected to raise US$2 billion this year, while there are good prospects for renewal of the PBoC swap line falling due mid-2026. Argentina has demonstrated a genuine capacity for fiscal dis- cipline that markets underestimated as recently as two years ago. records.text: Our thoughts on USD, HUF, AUD & NZD, CHF, COP , and CAD USD: Not just a case of open and shut. The Dollar weakened over the course of n the week on familiar drivers, including hopes of a US-Iran deal and steady CNY appreciation. Relative terms of trade continue to be a strong determinant of FX returns, and the FX market remains highly correlated and exceptionally stable. Leaning on these tendencies, we have highlighted a slate of crosses that we think are best to position for resolution or escalation, especially where it aligns with other fundamentals: those include ZAR, HUF, KRW and CLP in EM alongside SEK, NZD and GBP in the G10 space. That said, we see a number of hurdles for the broad Dollar to “snap back” to the overwhelmingly negative narrative that prevailed in January and February. We believe there are two important shifts affecting broad terms of trade simultaneously—an AI boom and an energy supply bust—which are both net positive for the Dollar and help explain why it is 1-1.5% stronger (depending on the index) on net since the beginning of March. The AI boom has helped restore foreign investor demand for Dollar assets that we think was a critical component behind last year’s currency depreciation. Relatedly, it helps explain the divergent growth picture through easier financial conditions and stronger investment. records.text: sk of permanent substitution concentrated in China (Figures 5 & 6). • Petrochemicals are a harder case for substitution, because they run through supply chains in ways that are difficult to unwind. But even there, economies tend to adapt through efficiency gains, material substitution, and, at the margin, outright thrift. A small but telling example comes from Japanese snack maker Calbee. To help offset rising naphtha costs—a key petrochemical feedstock largely sourced from the Gulf—the company has temporarily shifted 14 of its iconic products (including potato chips) to black-and-white packaging. The move will likely be reversed once naphtha supplies normalize, not least because it imposes a real friction on consumers. Without the familiar color-coding (orange for lightly salted, green for seaweed), shoppers have to slow down and scrutinize labels, relying on text rather than instant visual cues to quickly grab their favorite flavors. That distinction matters. Measures like this reflect cost pass-through and short-term coping strategies more than a durable rewriting of demand. For that reason, we assume most of the roughly 2.4 mbd of lost petrochemical feedstock demand is likely to return as supply conditions normalize. • Jet fuel is the clearest case of the roughly 500 kbd demand loss that should mostly recover once supply chains stabilize. records.text: As the energy crisis continues, the Italian economy is showing no signs of idiosyncratic deterioration. We forecast economic growth to be among the lowest in the Euro area, but with fiscal deficit targets still contained, the Italian sovereign spread continues to price a weakening European economy and does not reflect idiosyncratic risk. Our updated model, a simple structural vector autoregression (SVAR) analysis with “sign restrictions”, decomposes the Italian sovereign spread (10y BTP-Bund) into European risk, Domestic Risk and a broad rates sell-off. We find that investors are growing increasingly wary of the deteriorating momentum in the European economy but still assign no role to risk factors specific to the Italian landscape, usually connected to rising front and long ends of the yield curve and a widening sovereign spread (Exhibit 3). For the Fed to hike sooner than we anticipate, labor markets would need to tighten decisively. In that vein, while it is encouraging that the pace of payroll growth has firmed YTD, a host of high- er-frequency labor market indicators suggest the unemployment rate should remain stable around 4.3%, still above the Fed’s 4.2% NAIRU forecast (see US: Jobless claims still look- ing fine, Abiel Reinhart, 5/28/26). Additionally, a favorable carry profile supports staying long. As we highlighted two weeks ago, the repricing in front-end yields has left risk-adjusted carry markedly improved versus where it was even a month ago, and this profile is superior relative to the rest of the Treasury curve as well (Figure 4T h e f r o n t e n d o f f e r s s u p e r i o r r i s k - a d j u s t e d c a r r y ). records.text: European Economic Perspectives1 June 2026 ab 5 European Economic Perspectives UBS Research BoE Next meeting: 18 June; Bank Rate currently at 3.75% Market view: Markets are pricing +1.5bp for June; total hikes of 33.7bp by end-26 UBS view: Rates on hold with the next move being a cut (Feb and Apr-27), not a hike As firmly expected, the BoE left Bank Rate unchanged at 3.75% at its last meeting on 30 April. The decision was supported by 8 MPC members with only Huw Pill voting for a 25bp rate hike. Overall, the Committee reiterated its message from the previous meeting that it “stands ready to act as necessary to ensure that CPI inflation remains on track to meet the 2% target in the medium term”, implying that all options remain open. The Bank also presented three scenarios with varying assumptions about the severity and persistence of the energy shock and strength of potential second-round effects. Despite scenarios using the market-implied path for Bank Rate, implying some hikes, the Bank effectively viewed the tightening in financial conditions since their last projections update in February as already providing a sufficient policy response without them actually hiking rates in all but more adverse, persistent energy scenario. That said, the Governor described the decision as an "active" hold and emphasised that the trajectory going forward will greatly depend on the evolution of the conflict, hence, not ruling out rate hikes going forward. Tourism—potentially more exchange-rate-sensi- tive—accounts for about 39% of services, while transport ser- vices (around 40%) are linked to aviation and logistics, which are less likely to be driven by local-currency fluctuations. Ginnie calculates its de minimis contribution by looking at the UPB of the loans excluding upfront MIPs/funding fees. However, in the MBS data we only see the UPB inclusive of those capitalized fees. That difference matters because loans that are on the cusp of the superconforming threshold would get counted using the UPB including the MIPs/funding fees, but not be counted by Ginnie for the 10% servicer cap. There’s also the consideration that upfront fees on purchase V A loans (at 2.15%) can be larger than pur- chase FHA loans (at 1.75%) and generally larger than refis (0.5% for a V A IRRRL and for FHA refis, the 1.75% upfront MIP minus the reimbursement schedule based on age). This means that it can appear from the MBS data that a particular issuer has gone over the 10% limit when it’s plausible that there’s just some noise around funding fees. In any event, the issuers who push up against the de minimis limit naturally tend to be the ones that issue the most MJMs (Figure 20… a n d t h e s e s a m e s e r v i c e r s t e n d t o b e t h e l a r g e s t i s s u e r s o f s u p e r c o n f o r m i n g l o a n s i n c u s t o m a n d j u m b o s p a c e ). records.text: igh for a prolonged period, the n government interest rate could eventually rise significantly and exceed the nominal GDP growth rate. In that case, the debt/GDP ratio would likely shift to a long-term upward trend earlier than we previously assumed. Assuming the government increases the defense budget to 3% of GDP and cuts the food consumption tax rate permanently, and further assuming that the 10-year market yield remains at 2.0% from now on, it would take about 15 years for the debt/GDP ratio to start rising. However, assuming a 10-year yield level of 2.7%, it would take about 10 years, and if the yield rose to 3.5%, the ratio would start rising in about 5 years. This suggests that if the financial market’s concerns about public finances are n disregarded, it could lead to a rise in the debt/GDP ratio through an increase in the risk premium. Put another way, market concerns about sustainability could actually worsen sustainability. records.text: Agency MBS: Prefer GN II/FN 4.0s swap over the GN II/FN 4.5s swap We find the GN II/FN 4.0s swap offers better relative value vs. the GN II/FN 4.5s n swap, within the Ginnie Mae (GN) and Fannie Mae (FN) complexes. In recent months, the GN II/FN 4.5s swap has benefited from a higher share of n refinance loans in recent GN II 4.5s issuance vs. FN 4.5s issuance. However, the mortgage rate back-up and seasonal increase in purchase issuance could change this trend in the coming months. We believe the larger deliverable float of recently produced GN II 4.5s compared n to FN 4.5s could exert downside pressure on the swap, especially vs. 4.0s where the size of the floats are more comparable between GNs and conventionals. RMBS: Lower prepayment risk driving prime jumbo outperformance The OAS differential of prime jumbo seniors relative to same-coupon FN TBAs n has tightened in recent months, driven by the back up in mortgage rates. Current differential is in line with fair value adjusted for collateral rate incentive. If mortgage rates hold steady, rising GWACs on future prime jumbo deal issuance n could drive the OAS/price differential vs. TBAs to tighten further. Figure 24:NEGU disbursements Source : EC, Macrobond, Deutsche Bank Research Although the energy crisis will weigh on Italy, the country can still draw support from NGEU. Fund disbursement is proceeding in line with the plan agreed with the EU. Italy has requested the ninth tranche, expected before the end of summer, and should request the tenth and final tranche by September. Together they total EUR 41bn, around 2% of GDP. Italy can also still use funds already disbursed but not yet spent. Of the roughly EUR 153bn disbursed by end-2025, only 53% had been spent, leaving about EUR 72bn, or 3.5% of GDP, still to deploy. NGEU should therefore continue to support growth in 2026 and even more in 2027, especially if higher costs and supply bottlenecks delay projects this year. While growth in 2027 could exceed potential, 2028 warrants more caution, as the cyclical NGEU boost will have faded and its longer-term benefits may take more time to appear. records.text: 1 June 2026 World Outlook Deutsche Bank AG Page 19 Germany Summary. The Middle East conflict has presented the German economy with multifaceted headwinds. Growth momentum is therefore likely to weaken towards the middle of the year. If our geopolitical baseline materializes, the economy should pick up again by Q4, even if inflationary pressures are likely to subside only slowly. Expansionary fiscal policy is the decisive stabilizer, so GDP is forecast to grow by 0.5% in 2026. By 2027, we expect a normalization of the external environment and a fiscal- led domestic recovery, lifting GDP growth to 1.3%. Growth. Following a robust Q1, the economy is projected to contract slightly in Q2 and stagnate in Q3. Should a peace resolution in the Middle East materialize by June, it will nonetheless take some time until price pressures in various pockets abate. Consequently, cost-related headwinds and inflation-induced weakening of private consumption will persist into the second half of 2026. records.text: 10 “The Path to 2075 — Slower Global Growth, But Convergence Remains Intact”, Goldman Sachs Global Box 1: The Path to 2075 — Long-Term Projections for the Global Economy The Path to 2075 projections builds on our original BRICs analysis, offering long-term forecasts for the global economy, covering 104 countries out to the year 2075.10 Exhibit 6 provides a high-level summary of our projections for the major regional aggregates, broken down by decade. Our projections imply that global growth in 2024-29 (2.8%) will be faster than in 2020-24, but slower than in the 2010-19 decade (3.2%, based on market FX weights).11 We project that EM growth will continue to outstrip DM growth (3.8% vs. 1.8%), with around half of this difference due to demographic factors and the other half due to productivity growth differentials. We expect Asia (ex-DM) to remain the fastest-growing region. Exhibit 7 combines our GDP estimates with our long-term real exchange rate projections, to project the real US Dollar value of major economies over time. In 2050, we project that the world’s five largest economies will be China, the US, India, Indonesia, and Germany (with Indonesia displacing Brazil and Russia among the list of largest EMs over this horizon). We estimate that China will overtake the US as the world’s largest economy around 2035.12 If we extend the projection horizon to 2075, the world’s three largest economies are China, India, and the US, with India ( just) overtaking the US. The bank highlighted that the stronger forint, along with the postponed phase-out of regulated fuel prices and price margin caps, is helping to contain price pressures. Against this backdrop, we now expect the NBH to deliver 25bp cuts in June and September (vs one cut in September previously). Conditional on further normalisation in energy prices, an additional 25bp cut in H2 26 is also possible. In South Africa, the SARB hiked by 25bp to 7.00%, supported by four members of the MPC committee, while two voted to hold. This was a somewhat less hawkish distribution than we had projected, as we had expected at least one member to vote for a 50bp hike, given the recent jump in inflation. The SARB also revised its medium-term forecasts: downward for growth (by 0.5pp to 1.2% y/y for 2026 and 0.3pp to 1.5% y/y for 2027) and up for inflation. It now expects CPI to average 4.4% in 2026, 3.7% in 2027 and 3% in 2028, which is broadly in line with our respective estimates of 4.4%, 3.9% and 3%. We suspect the 20bp gap between its 2027 forecast (3.7%) and ours (3.9%) is due largely to different oil price assumptions. We expect inflation to accelerate further, and thus continue to expect one more hike, in July, taking the terminal policy rate to 7.25%. 29 May 2026 61 Barclays | Global Economics Weekly: Waiting for the deal

We forecast a 75k increase in both headline and private payrolls in May (consensus 93k), with the unemployment rate holding at 4.3% (consensus 4.3%). Barring revisions, this would place the 3mma at around 125k, and the 4mma at 55k—with the latter much closer to the view of underlying job gains that informs our baseline. With recent job gains greatly surpassing prevailing estimates that the breakeven pace is close to zero, many will be looking for signs in average hourly earnings that a pick-up in wage growth is taking shape. Should FX pressures sustain until the 18 June policy meeting, BI could feel compelled to deliver another larger-than-usual 50bp hike to demonstrate its resolve in defending the IDR. While this might run counter to the government's pro-growth agenda, we noted in Indonesia: Outsized 50bp hike (20 May 2026) that the 50bp hike on 20 May suggests that IDR depreciation has reached levels that have caused the government to relent on monetary policy tightening. As it did on 20 May, BI is likely to continue encouraging banks to not raise lending rates despite policy rate hikes, citing ample liquidity and macroprudential easing. Regardless of whether a 50bp policy rate hike does materialise on 18 June, we suspect BI would still eventually seek to pivot back towards rate cuts. In our current base case of a 25bp rate hike, to 5.50%, on 18 June, we have projected 25bp rate cuts in March, April and May 2027 – to 4.75% – in line with our forecast for a 25bp Fed funds rate cut in March 2027, though risks are tilted towards delays. A 50bp hike on 18 June instead of 25bp would likely imply one more 25bp cut is needed in June 2027 to eventually bring the policy rate back down to 4.75%. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 01 Jun 2026 08:15:44 ET │ 11 pages US Economics NFP Preview – Stability expected, but downside risks remain CITI'S TAKE We expect a third consecutive month of job growth in May, with nonfarm payroll employment rising by 60k jobs and the unemployment rate remaining at 4.3% (but alongside another drop in the labor force participation rate). Markets and Fed officials have come to expect stability in the labor market and a May report in line with our forecasts would likely have little implication for market pricing. But we would continue to caution that monthly payroll data have become more volatile this year (downside surprises are not unlikely) and substantial uncertainty around the labor force participation rate creates two-sided risks for the unemployment rate. Any sign of a weakening labor market (softer payrolls, higher unemployment) would likely elicit a larger market reaction, further pricing out rate hikes. Our base case remains for softer labor market data into the summer months and the Fed cutting rates in response. LLC US Daily: Slower Income Growth Means Slower Consumer Spending Growth This Year 31 May 2026 | 9:03PM EDT Real disposable personal income declined 1.1% year-over-year in April, n reflecting a combination of higher energy prices, tariff passthrough, and slowing wage growth. Real personal income excluding transfers—an NBER recession indicator—declined 1.0%, the weakest pace outside of recession except for a similarly-sized decline in June 2022 and a policy-induced drop in 2013. The decline in real personal income over the last year is somewhat exaggerated n because of policy-induced swings in Social Security and proprietors’ income. Slower immigration weighed on income growth too. But even after adjusting for these factors, real personal income per worker excluding transfers declined 0.6% over the last year, a pace rarely seen outside of recession. We expect higher energy prices will continue to erode household spending power for the rest of the year, and we forecast only 0.9% real income growth in 2026 on a Q4/Q4 basis. The slowdown in income growth has not yet translated into slower spending n growth, likely because OBBBA-related tax cuts have boosted consumer cashflow since the start of the year and because consumers have offset the hit to income by saving less. The crisis is now acting as an accelerant, reinforcing the shift through higher fuel costs, energy-security concerns, supportive policy, and the continued rapid expansion of charging infrastructure. We estimate China’s gasoline demand destruction at about 180 kbd, and expect 70% of that loss may not return even after markets normalize (Figures 3 & 4). The reason is simple: once consumers switch to EVs, the change tends to be sticky. Outside China, the structural effects are likely smaller but still meaningful. In Europe, new car registrations climbed to their highest level since 2019 in March, led by hybrids, which overtook diesel and petrol cars in late 2025. History suggests that past oil shocks often left lasting declines in gasoline demand, and this episode may prove no different. On that basis, we expect that some portion of the 900 kbd loss in gasoline demand may never fully return. Diesel shows a similar, if more uneven, risk profile. Part of the roughly 850 kbd decline in diesel demand may also prove durable, with the risk of permanent substitution concentrated in China (Figures 5 & 6). • Petrochemicals are a harder case for substitution, because they run through supply chains in ways that are difficult to unwind.
