Our cluster analysis uses daily FX data (using London 4pm fixing) across a six-month window. Clusters are aggregated using the distance function (1- correlation) and applying Ward’s clustering algorithm. We reduce the pool of currencies into those that are correlated with one another so as to better identify the factors that impact different ‘types’ of currency. The model then calculates uncorrelated factors that are important for each cluster (principal components 1, 2 and 3) using daily changes over a six-month window. We switch from weekly to daily changes to allow the model to capture greater variability and faster-changing patterns. From a list of around 70 market variables as well as some measures of economic activity such as data surprise and economic strength, the model finds the market variables that appear to represent these uncorrelated factors. We compute the correlation between each variable and the principal components over three windows (1.5 months, 3 months and 6 months) and then compute the average correlation over the three windows. records.text: Exhibit 4 shows the trend of the debt/GDP ratio under the three scenarios above, assuming that market interest rates as of May 25 remain constant. As Exhibit 2 shows, the natural decline in the debt/GDP ratio from the “r - g” effect would eventually turn into a natural increase as the government’s average interest rate rises, and the larger the primary deficit, the sooner the ratio would start to rise. Exhibit 5 shows how the debt/GDP ratio would change under different market interest rates, assuming a primary balance deficit at the level incorporating an increase in defense spending to 3% of GDP and permanent implementation of a food consumption tax cut (dotted lines in Exhibit 3 and Exhibit 4). Assuming the interest rate from the end of 2025, when the 10-year yield was at 2.0%, it would take about 15 years for the debt/GDP ratio to start rising. However, if the interest rates as of May 25 were to persist, it would take about 10 years, and assuming the 10-year yield rose to 3.5%, the ratio would start rising in about 5 years. These exhibits show that while a rise in market interest rates would not cause a major change in the trend of the debt/GDP ratio in the short term, its long-term impact would be very significant. This suggests that disregarding the financial market’s concerns about public finances could lead to a rise in the debt/GDP ratio via an increase in the term premium. records.text: 1 June 2026 World Outlook Deutsche Bank AG Page 33 Rates We have revised our forecast for the US 10-year Treasury up to 4.70% and, more marginally, the 10-year Bund forecast up to 3.20%. The upward revisions reflect a Fed on hold and the front-loading of ECB hikes in Europe. The 5s10s term premia assumptions remain broadly unchanged, save for some technical adjustments. The main downside risks to the view are (1) both tails on AI (a bubble or higher unemployment) and (2) materially lower oil prices on the back of a comprehensive resolution to the Iran war. In our 2026 outlook, we expected a mild sell-off in UST and EUR bond markets, with the 10y US Treasury reaching 4.45% and the 10y Bund reaching 3.10%. Our forecast reflected structural and cyclical factors supporting higher yields, tempered by the risks and uncertainties associated with AI and, at the time, perceived downside risks to oil prices. Six months on, the US data have been broadly supportive of higher equilibrium rates, with, amongst other factors, evidence of significant AI-related capex and upside risks to US fiscal deficits. Moreover, the Fed Senior Loan Officer Survey and financial conditions provide further confirmation that US monetary policy is unlikely to be tight. Not only did the downside risks to oil prices fail to materialise, but the Iran war has resulted in sharply higher commodity prices. Payroll gains have firmed on balance in recent months, and the breadth of those gains has improved. Measures of labor market slack have also been stable for more than a year. Our baseline is that the unemployment rate remains close to current levels (~4.3%) through 2026 and will decline slightly next year. For the first time in a while, risks appear more balanced. records.text: s decision to leave the OPEC alliance at the start of May 2026 (link). While the immediate macro impact is limited given the ongoing closure of the Hormuz Strait, the ability to produce more oil could influence the future structure of the UAE economy. With authorities targeting 5mbpd by 2027 and projects that could raise capacity further to 6mbpd (link), the hydrocarbon sector is likely to record strong growth in the coming years. At the same time, we believe the conflict could leave lasting scars on key non-hydrocarbon sectors. Hospitality, real estate, construction, transport, and logistics could all struggle to return to their prior growth rates. The UAE’s non-oil econo- my had been expanding rapidly, with growth above 6% over the past five years and around 4% over the past 15 years. We now assume a more conservative potential growth rate of around 2%–3%. This view remains highly uncertain given the ongoing disruption, the lack of a full conflict resolution, and the difficulty of forming firm assumptions about the region’s longer-term outlook. Under these assumptions, we expect the hydrocarbon sector to reverse the trend of recent decades, with hydrocarbons potentially rising to around 29% of the UAE economy by 2028—around 4pp higher than in 2025. records.text: Global Equity Strategy1 June 2026 ab 7 Middle East: Surprisingly, we fielded only 1 question on this. An interesting question is what happens once Iranian storage reaches capacity. Is this the point at which we may see more compromise? Oil: The consensus view is that oil will be higher for longer because of the geopolitical risk premium and the need to rebuild inventories. Hence, UBS forecast end 2026 Brent at $90/bbl and the Brent futures 1 year forward is up 30% since 27 February. Some (like us) see the risk that once the conflict is over, the market will refocus on fundamentals, i.e., back to the market that was in place in December 2025 where excess capacity in OPEC was c4Mb/d (sufficient to restock the lost barrels within a year). Moreover, there is a long term upside risk on supply both from a settlement (especially from Venezuela and Iran - recall, under the Shah, Iran produced 5.8Mb/d cf to 3.5Mb/d pre-conflict), and from UAE withdrawing from OPEC. At the same time, there exists downside risks to demand (with the rise in renewables and EVs owing to the Middle East crisis and a drive towards energy independence outside the US). Interestingly, the oil stocks now appear to be looking through the oil price. There appears to be a risk this time, that into a bear market, OPEC discipline might be reduced as concerns about stranded assets could encourage producers to monetise reserves. records.text: we anticipate a moderate pickup later in the year and into 2027. ▪ Unemployment rate stable at 4.3%, risk s balanced: One knock against April’s report was that if the participation rate had held steady, the unemployment rate would have risen to 4.5% instead of holding at 4.3%. We pencil in a rounded 0.1pp rise in participation for May, which also implies that the household survey employment number should look better than the payroll figure after trailing it for several months. Youth unemployment – a job market canary: We see younger workers as a key gauge of the net effect of two cross currents in the US economy: the diffusion of artificial intelligence tools (which looks set to displace employees in some industries) and cyclical resilience in activity coupled with AI optimism (which we think is likely to increase demand for labor). records.text: 29 May 2026 UK Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 The vacancy yield. We construct another alternative for labour market matching – the vacancy yield rate. This is defined as hires (i.e. gross employee inflows) per vacancy (or the inverse of time-to-fill). The vacancy yield measures how efficiently posted vacancies convert into filled positions. A declining yield means firms are posting more vacancies to achieve the same number of hires — a direct measure of match quality deterioration. A rising yield suggests that employers are finding it easier to fill vacancies. The strongest reason to use such a measure is that it cuts through the noise of headline vacancy counts. If yields are recovering toward pre-pandemic norms, it's a concrete signal that the matching function is improving. As of March 2026, we estimate the vacancy yield to have risen to 81% – a big jump from the lows seen the aftermath of the pandemic (which dropped to as low as 52%). Labour Market Mismatch Index (DB). As our final measure of labour market matching, we update our own labour market mismatch index (LMMI). This measures dispersion between where jobs are and where workers are — across sectors, occupations or regions. The absolute difference between aggregate vacancy and unemployment rates captures how "out of sync" supply and demand are. A narrowing spread equals better matching. Where is our LMMI tracking? At 0.116 – near its cyclical lows. Which industries are showing the least amount of mismatches?

Prepayment volatility can create nega- tive carry if bond coupons exceed asset earnings, accelerate reinvest- ment risk, and introduce timing mis- matches around redemption dates and distribution cycles. Over time, these dynamics can erode coverage even in the absence of borrower defaults. Reserves Reserves are usually evaluated rela- tive to the structure’s timing risk, including capitalized interest and any debt service reserve fund, and the accessibility of those funds when needed. Reserves are a first-line buffer for tim- ing mismatch and operational disrup- tion. Under Moody’s methodology, reserve weakness can contribute to rating outcomes below the highest eli- gible level. Beyond these five areas, additional structural protections that typically merit review include restrictions on trustee acceleration on covenant breaches (limited to situations with 100% bondholder approval or sufficient funds to make bondholders whole), provisions that trustee resignation does not take effect until a successor is in place, and requirements that updated cash flow projections be produced any time additional bonds are issued within an existing transaction. Core pressures are also building amid fertilizer-driven food price spillovers. Moreover, tighter labor markets, firm pricing power, and potential El Niño-related climate shocks add upside risk. • Central banks’ narrative has shifted decisively hawkish given the size and persistence of the oil/energy shock. In Europe, we expect the ECB to hike in June, and the BoE to hike in July, while in the US we expect the Fed to shift to a neutral bias at their June meeting. • We analyze the empirical “convexity optimism” across asset classes, manifesting itself in larger risk-on reaction to positive headlines (falling Brent prices) versus risk-off reaction to negative headlines (rising Brent prices), and likely driven by persistent expectations of a resolution in the conflict. This convexity dynamic vs. oil price change is stronger for AI- driven equity indices, US high-yield and EM sovereign credit, and high- yielding currencies, on the back of idiosyncratic drivers (1Q earnings, Anthropic’s Mythos, computational demand, energy exporters, and FX carry). • Cross Asset Views – The strong fundamental backdrop remains intact and supports our bullish stance on risk assets.

Security, insurance and mine clearing: The first hurdle to overcome is for shipowners and insurance providers to regain confidence that the Strait is genuinely safe to navigate again. In itself, the announcement of a ceasefire extension is not necessarily sufficient for that. The market needs evidence that attacks, tolling, or interdictions will not resume. As part of this, the area needs to be cleared from sea mines. As long as sea mines are believed to be in place in the traditional shipping lanes, the capacity of the Strait is much reduced, even if it's technically 'open'. The time it takes for the area to be cleared for mines is uncertain but likely in the order of weeks to several months. 2. Tanker backlog and vessel misallocation: Then, tankers are in the wrong place. Over the last few months, idle ships that couldn't find work in the area, ballasted to the US Gulf, West Africa, Brazil, etc, often creating an oversupply there. On its 1Q26 earnings call, Aramco's CEO called this "the biggest issue", adding that "even in the most optimistic scenario, the energy and commodity supply chains will need several months to return to their pre-conflict traffic, as vessels reroute or avoid being idle". There are a number of 'empties' parked just outside the Gulf, so some initial cargoes could move quickly. G10 consumers n generally continue to benefit from healthy balance sheets, but labor markets are more mixed, sentiment has worsened from already low levels following the start of the war in the Middle East, and we expect spending headwinds as higher energy prices erode real incomes in the next few months. Household balance sheets remain strong. Household net worth as a share of n income stands close to all time highs in the US, Japan and Australia, is around percentile 90 (P90) in Canada and the Euro area, and stands around P65 in the UK. Since we last published the dashboard, real net worth growth was little changed at P65 in the US and Japan (P65), P50 in the Euro area, and P40 in the UK, Canada and Australia. The saving rate declined to its lowest level since June 2022 in the US, and also declined in Canada (but remains elevated). Elsewhere, the saving rate remains elevated outside of Japan (Exhibit 10). Consumer sentiment remains below its historical average across the G10 n (Exhibit 13). records.text: US Outlook Consumers feeling the strain Pressures on household purchasing power have intensified amid elevated inflation and slowing labor income. While spending is beginning to soften, carryover effects should support Q2 growth. With investment providing an offset and inflation still elevated, the Fed remains poised for an extended hold. • Consumers are slowing at the margin, but underlying demand remains firm. Q1 GDP was revised down to 1.6% q/q saar, but PDFP held at 2.4%, with AI-driven capex offsetting softer consumption and leaving the Fed focused on resilient private demand rather than headline weakness. This helps explain why FOMC participants are unlikely to be stirred by near-term growth softness. • Purchasing power strains are becoming clearer. April’s saving rate fell 0.6pp (down 1.7pp since January), reflecting spending running ahead of income amid elevated inflation and slowing labor income—though Q2 spending growth will be supported by carryover effects from earlier gains. As elevated inflation persists, consumers are likely to shift from lower saving to slower consumption. • Core PCE price inflation has softened, but for reasons the Fed is likely to discount. April’s rate slowed to 0.24% m/m (3.3% y/y), but much of this reflected financial services categories that are poised to reverse, even as pressures from AI-related goods persist. For the time being, risks remain that underlying inflation will run faster than the 2% target, reinforcing the Fed’s hold. Hand

Core inflation rose by just 0.06% on the month in April on a non- seasonally adjusted basis, and the annual rate slowed to 1.5% from 1.9% in March. The Bank of Canada’s preferred core measures also moderated in April. The trimmed mean fell by 0.2pp to 2.0% year on year, while the weighted median fell by 0.2pp to 2.1%. Bank of Canada on hold Taken together, weaker growth, a soft labour market and subdued core inflation all support our view that the Bank of Canada will remain on hold. Despite firmer headline inflation, we think the BoC will look through the energy-driven rise given the risk of worsening an already fragile growth backdrop. We would also view the risks to rates in 2026 as tilted to the downside. If the USMCA renegotiation proves more prolonged than expected, the BoC may yet need to ease rather than tighten policy if domestic demand weakens further. Further ahead, if the USMCA review is resolved, or if there is at least greater clarity on the likely path, whether that means a deal or a shift to annual reviews, stronger growth should support firmer core inflation and increase the likelihood of hikes. We see that as a second-half 2027 story. As a closed-loop system that must clear daily, the oil market can only adjust through some combination of inventory draws and demand loss. Supply to the market fell by roughly 12.6 mbd in March, 14.1 mbd in April, and 16.4 mbd in May. These losses were offset through a mix of inventory draws—about 3 mbd in March, 6.5 mbd in April, and 7.4 mbd in May —alongside demand declines of roughly 2.8 mbd, 4.3 mbd, and 5.6 mbd over the same months, respectively. The lessons of the 1973 oil shock are instructive precisely because the world today looks fundamentally different from the one that entered the first oil embargo. In 1973, oil was deeply embedded across nearly every part of the global economy: electricity generation was heavily oil-dependent, vehicle efficiency was poor, public transportation infrastructure was limited, and large-scale alternatives barely existed. The result was a severe macroeconomic shock that triggered recession, inflation, industrial weakness, and a lasting restructuring of global energy systems. Much of the modern energy system was built in direct response to those vulnerabilities. In the US, the crisis led to the creation of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the establishment of the Department of Energy, the introduction of fuel economy standards, and even the national 55 mph speed limit aimed at reducing gasoline consumption.
